Confusing glinting with glittering, which implies many sparkles rather than one flash.

senses.definition: The major protein in cereal grains, especially wheat; responsible for the elasticity in dough and the structure in baked bread.
A gluey, sticky mass of clay, bitumen etc.
senses.example: The old kiln workers scraped a gluey gluten of clay from the wheel before it hardened.

senses.definition: (rare) Any gluey, sticky substance.
senses.example: The glue-like gluten coated the wooden toys, leaving a sticky residue on every surface.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A protein in wheat and related grains that gives bread dough its elasticity and chewy structure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced, unstressed 'tun', not a clear 'ten', so do not say GLOO-ten.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in cooking and baking. In health contexts it can carry a sense of caution or restriction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gluten constantly on food labels, menus, and in diet talk, such as gluten-free, contains gluten, or gluten intolerance. For a diagnosed celiac disease, the reaction is medical and serious, so people with it avoid gluten strictly. A casual 'I'm gluten-free' is common in restaurants, where staff will often ask about it.

distinctions.note: Wheat is the grain itself; gluten is one protein in it, and it also occurs in barley and rye.
Glutinous means sticky or gluey; it shares the root with gluten but is an everyday descriptive adjective, not the name of the protein.
Celiac disease is a diagnosed autoimmune reaction triggered by gluten, while gluten sensitivity is a broader, less precisely defined term.

examples.everyday: Can you check whether the soup has gluten? My sister can't have it.
examples.professional: We need a gluten-free label on the new packaging, so the lab has to confirm the test results first.
examples.analytical: Dough's elasticity depends on gluten forming a network that traps the gas from yeast, which is why bakers knead it.

nuance.analogy: Gluten is the scaffolding inside bread dough: a web that holds the air in place while the loaf rises.
nuance.etymology: From Latin gluten, meaning glue.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'ten' instead of a reduced 'tun'.
Saying I'm allergic to gluten when the condition is celiac disease or intolerance; allergy and celiac are different medical categories.

gluten.etymology: From Middle French *gluten*, borrowed from Latin *glūten* (“glue”).

senses.definition: Inviting someone to speak first.

core.definition: A polite way to invite someone to speak or act first, meaning you may begin or you have permission to continue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'head', the second syllable of 'ahead'. The first word 'go' is lighter. In fast speech, 'go ahead' sounds like 'guh-HED'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it is a friendly and courteous way to give someone the floor or permission.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Go ahead' constantly in meetings, on the phone, and in daily life. It is polite and natural in almost any setting. In a meeting, you might say 'Go ahead, you first' to let someone speak. A natural reply is 'Thanks' or 'Thanks, I was going to ask the same thing'.

distinctions.note: 'Go ahead' gives permission or invites someone to begin, while 'Go on' often encourages someone to continue talking or expresses disbelief.
'Be my guest' is more hospitable and warm, while 'Go ahead' is a simpler and more neutral way to give permission.

collocations: Go ahead and start without me

examples.everyday: You want to take the last slice of pizza? Go ahead, I'm full.
examples.professional: Go ahead and share your screen when you are ready, and we will review the model results.
examples.analytical: When a philosopher says 'go ahead' to an objection, she is granting the floor while keeping the argument under her control.

nuance.analogy: It is like a traffic light turning green: you have permission to move forward.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Go ahead to' before a noun instead of using 'Go ahead with' or 'Go ahead and'.
Stressing 'go' equally with 'ahead' so the phrase sounds flat.
Using it as a question with rising intonation when a statement with falling intonation is more natural.

conversation.text: Go ahead and start eating, don't wait for me.
"Can I borrow your pen?" "Sure, go ahead."
You go ahead, I'll meet you at the restaurant.
The project finally went ahead after months of delays.
We got the go-ahead from finance, so we can order the laptops.
Don't start the redesign until we get the go-ahead from the client.
"Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt." "No, go ahead."
Go ahead, Ana. You had your hand up first.
Sorry, I'm talking too much. Go ahead, James.

senses.definition: To forgo (something).
senses.example: If you forgot to bring your toothpaste, you'll have to go without.

senses.definition: To lack or be deprived of (something).
senses.example: The poor man's children went without supper.

core.definition: To be without something you need or want, or to choose not to have it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OUT in without, and the th is voiceless as in thin. Do not stress the first syllable of without, and make the ou a clear diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can be negative when describing deprivation and positive when describing voluntary restraint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go without' for both necessity and choice, as in 'We went without heat for two days' or 'I can go without coffee today.' When describing hardship, it often implies a lack of basic things. In casual speech, people might say 'I can do without' for a voluntary choice. A natural reply is 'Wow, that sounds tough.'

distinctions.note: Do without is very close in meaning and is slightly more common for voluntary choices, while go without often describes a lack that is harder to avoid.
Lack is a formal or neutral noun or verb for not having something, and it sounds more analytical than go without.

examples.everyday: We had to go without a car for a month while ours was in the shop.
examples.professional: The team cannot go without a clear owner for the data pipeline, so we need to assign one this week.
examples.analytical: Many thinkers argue that a person cannot go without some sense of meaning and still remain fully human.

nuance.analogy: Like walking a long road with an empty bag, carrying nothing you wish you had.
common_mistakes: Using 'go without' with 'of', as in 'go without of heat'; the phrase takes the thing directly.
Confusing it with 'go without it' versus 'go without doing it', which is a different structure.

conversation.text: We went without power for two days after the storm.
I can't go without coffee in the morning.

senses.definition: A monetary system where the value of circulating money is linked to the value of gold.
senses.example: Many economists argue that leaving the gold standard eased the recovery of the 1930s.

senses.definition: The highest or most reliable benchmark against which all others in a category are judged or measured.
senses.example: The OED is the gold standard for English dictionaries.

core.definition: The most reliable and highest benchmark against which other things in a category are judged or measured.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, STAN, with a short a as in cat. The final syllable is reduced to a soft er sound, and the last d is clear, so do not say stan-dard with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying excellence and reliability; can be used ironically if the benchmark is questionable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gold standard for the best benchmark in medicine, science, business, and everyday praise, as in the gold standard for pie. The monetary sense, a currency backed by gold, is mostly historical, so mentioning it in conversation may sound like an economics lesson. A natural reply to a compliment is something like yeah, it's the gold standard.

distinctions.note: A benchmark is any measure used for comparison, while a gold standard is the best and most trusted one in its field.
Best practice describes a recommended method, while gold standard describes a top reference point, often a specific test, study, or product.

examples.everyday: My sister's pie is the gold standard for Thanksgiving, so I always bring something else.
examples.professional: A randomized controlled trial is the gold standard for testing whether a new feature really improves retention.
examples.analytical: Rigorous source criticism became the gold standard of historical scholarship, though later historians questioned some of its assumptions.

nuance.analogy: A gold standard is the master yardstick kept in a vault, and every other measure is checked against it.
nuance.etymology: From gold and standard; the monetary sense dates to the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Using gold standard only for money; in everyday American English it usually means the best benchmark.
Pronouncing standard with a long a, like STAYND-ard, instead of the short a in STAN.

senses.definition: Of a person or an animal:
senses.example: good intentions

senses.definition: Acting in the interest of what is beneficial, ethical, or moral.
senses.example: good intentions

senses.definition: Competent or talented.
senses.example: a good swimmer

senses.definition: Able to be depended on for the discharge of obligations incurred; of unimpaired credit; used with for.
senses.example: Can you lend me fifty dollars? You know I'm good for it.

senses.definition: Well-behaved (especially of children or animals).
senses.example: Be good while your mother and I are out.

senses.definition: Satisfied or at ease; not requiring more.
senses.example: Would you like a glass of water? — I'm good.

senses.definition: Accepting of, OK with.
senses.example: My mother said she's good with me being alone with my date as long as she's met them first.

senses.definition: Of a capability:
senses.example: it’s a good watch; the flashlight batteries are still good

senses.definition: Useful for a particular purpose; functional.
senses.example: it’s a good watch; the flashlight batteries are still good

senses.definition: Effective.
senses.example: a good worker

senses.definition: Of a property or quality:
senses.example: The food was very good.

senses.definition: Of food:
senses.example: The food was very good.

senses.definition: Having a particularly pleasant taste.
senses.example: The food was very good.

senses.definition: Being satisfying; meeting dietary requirements.
senses.example: Eat a good dinner so you will be ready for the big game tomorrow.

senses.definition: Of food or other perishable products, still fit for use; not yet expired, stale, rotten, etc.
senses.example: The bread is still good.

senses.definition: Valid, of worth, capable of being honoured.
senses.example: This coupon is good for a free doughnut.

senses.definition: True, valid, of explanatory strength.
senses.example: This theory still holds good even if much higher temperatures are assumed.

senses.definition: Right, proper, as it should be.
senses.example: Please make sure the lab coats are hung up in good order before you leave.

senses.definition: Healthful.
senses.example: Exercise and a varied diet are good for you.

senses.definition: Pleasant; enjoyable.
senses.example: We had a good time.

senses.definition: Favorable.
senses.example: a good omen; good weather

senses.definition: Unblemished; honorable.
senses.example: a person's good name

senses.definition: Beneficial; worthwhile.
senses.example: a good job

senses.definition: Adequate; sufficient; not fallacious.
senses.example: The old bridge is still good for light trucks, though not for heavy loads.

senses.definition: Very, extremely. See good and.
senses.example: The soup is good and hot.

senses.definition: Ready.
senses.example: I'm good when you are.

senses.definition: Holy.
senses.example: Good Friday, Good Wednesday, the Good Book

senses.definition: Of a quantity:
senses.example: all in good time

senses.definition: Reasonable in amount.
senses.example: all in good time

senses.definition: Large in amount or size.
senses.example: a good while longer

senses.definition: Full; entire; at least as much as.
senses.example: This hill will take a good hour and a half to climb.

senses.definition: Special, best, favorite.
senses.example: No, not that one. That's my good shirt I only wear for special occasions.

senses.definition: Of a black person, dead or killed.
That is good; an elliptical exclamation of satisfaction or commendation.
senses.example: Good! I can leave now.

senses.definition: Well; satisfactorily or thoroughly.
senses.example: When you're cleaning these racks, you've got to get in there good, because the quality system specifies it.

senses.definition: The forces or behaviors that are the enemy of evil. Usually consists of helping others and general benevolence.
senses.example: The novel is a struggle between good and evil in a small mountain town.

senses.definition: A result that is positive in the view of the speaker.
senses.example: Despite the setbacks, the trial produced some good for the patients.

senses.definition: The abstract instantiation of goodness; that which possesses desirable qualities, promotes success, welfare, or happiness, is serviceable, fit, excellent, kind, benevolent, etc.
senses.example: The best is the enemy of the good.

senses.definition: An item of merchandise.
senses.example: The merchant displayed his goods in the market, hoping to sell everything before dark.

senses.definition: An article of personal property (as opposed to real property).
senses.example: Under the will, the house went to his son, while his personal goods went to his wife.

senses.definition: To thrive; fatten; prosper; improve.
senses.example: After the rains, the winter wheat began to good across the valley fields.

senses.definition: To make good; turn to good; improve.
senses.example: The company promised to good the damage it caused to the river.

senses.definition: To make improvements or repairs.
senses.example: The landlord agreed to good the broken windows before the tenants moved in.

senses.definition: To benefit; gain.
senses.example: The new policy did little to good the families who needed help most.

senses.definition: To do good to (someone); benefit; cause to improve or gain.
senses.example: Her steady mentoring goods every junior engineer who joins the team.

senses.definition: To satisfy; indulge; gratify.
senses.example: He loved to good his sweet tooth with a slice of pie after dinner.

senses.definition: To flatter; congratulate oneself; anticipate.
senses.example: He would good himself on his clever solution, though nobody else had noticed.

core.definition: Of high quality or a satisfactory standard; pleasant; or morally right, kind and beneficial to others.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like the vowel in 'book', not the long oo of 'food'. End with a clear d sound, and do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses approval, satisfaction, or moral praise, and it is one of the most flexible words in everyday American English.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use good constantly for everything from food and weather to behavior and health. Good is the usual reply to How are you?, and I'm good often means 'no thanks' or 'I'm fine.' Good for you can sound condescending when it praises an adult's ordinary choice, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Good is an adjective, while well is an adverb; say 'she speaks English well', not 'she speaks English good'. Well is also the usual word for health.
Nice is weaker and friendlier, describing pleasant things or people; good often implies quality, skill or moral worth.
Fine is more neutral and sometimes lukewarm, suggesting acceptable; good suggests a stronger, more positive judgment.

examples.everyday: Hey, this coffee smells good, thanks for making it.
examples.professional: The sales numbers look good, so let's keep the current budget for next quarter.
examples.analytical: A good argument is one whose premises give real reasons to accept its conclusion, not merely one that flatters the listener.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned instrument: it does exactly what it is meant to do.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gōd, from a Germanic root meaning fitting or suitable.
common_mistakes: Using good as an adverb, as in 'she plays good'; use well.
Using good to mean healthy, as in 'I am good now'; in careful speech, say well or fine.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word tov means good in the sense of pleasant, fitting, or beneficial, and the Greek agathos means good in the sense of beneficial and upright. Genesis 1:31 says God saw all he had made and found it very good. Mark 10:18 records Jesus asking why a man called him good, since no one is good but God alone. Romans 12:21 urges believers to overcome evil with good.

good.etymology: Middle English *good*, from Old English *gōd*, from **gōd*, from Proto-Germanic **gōdaz* (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʰedʰ-* (“to unite, be associated, suit, fit”).

senses.definition: The plant, a vine of genus Vitis, on which grapes grow.
senses.example: Although many grapevines have geographical names, these rarely reflect their real origin, if known at all.

senses.definition: An informal person-to-person means of circulating information or gossip.
senses.example: I heard through the grapevine that Jim will be leaving soon.

senses.definition: A move in which the feet are alternately placed in front of each other, while both remaining on the ice or ground, incorporating half-turns.
senses.example: The skater performed a grapevine across the ice, crossing her feet with smooth half-turns.

senses.definition: A leglock.
senses.example: In the final round, he trapped his opponent's legs in a grapevine until the referee intervened.

senses.definition: A dance figure in partner dancing that includes sidesteps and steps across the support foot. See Grapevine (dance move).
senses.example: The instructor taught us a grapevine with sidesteps, then a cross step on the support foot.

senses.definition: To restrain in a leglock.
senses.example: The wrestler grapevined his rival's legs, pinning him helplessly to the mat.

senses.definition: To drape or curl around adjacent objects.
senses.example: Wild vines had grapevined around the porch railings, curling tightly through every gap.

senses.definition: To move one's body in a smooth undulating wave while stepping in the direction the wave is moving.
senses.example: She grapevined her hips smoothly as the music swelled, stepping sideways with each wave.

senses.definition: To score mortar at a joint.
senses.example: The mason grapevined the fresh mortar joints with a tool to create a decorative pattern.

senses.definition: Of information, to spread as a rumor.
senses.example: Word of the layoffs grapevined through the office before lunch, though nobody had confirmed it.

senses.definition: Of a person or group, to spread (a rumor).
senses.example: Several coworkers grapevined the story about the merger until everyone in the building knew it.

senses.definition: To link up through an informal communication network.
senses.example: Volunteers grapevined through church networks to find housing for the displaced families.

core.definition: An informal network through which news and gossip spread from person to person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GRAPE. The second word, vine, has a long i like fine. Say the compound as one unit, running the p into the v, and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in itself, but it suggests unofficial talk, so the news it carries may be unreliable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grapevine mostly in the idiom I heard it through the grapevine, and at work people talk about the office grapevine when they mean unofficial news. It is casual and friendly, so it fits everyday talk and office chat, but not a formal announcement. A natural reply is Oh yeah? Who told you? or I hadn't heard that.

distinctions.note: A rumor is the unconfirmed news itself; the grapevine is the informal channel that carries it.
Gossip is idle talk about other people; grapevine names the network itself, which can carry news as well as gossip.

examples.everyday: I heard through the grapevine that you're moving to Denver. Is that true?
examples.professional: The reorganization isn't official yet, but the office grapevine already has the names.
examples.analytical: Informal networks like the grapevine often move information faster than formal channels, though with far less reliability.

nuance.analogy: Like a vine that spreads along fences in every direction, the grapevine carries news along paths nobody planned.
nuance.etymology: From grape plus vine; the 19th-century American phrase grapevine telegraph compared the tangled, indirect route of news to a vine.
common_mistakes: Using through the grapevine as in the grapevine; the standard idiom uses through.
Using grapevine for an official source; it names unofficial channels only.

senses.definition: To seize something and hold it firmly.
To wrestle or tussle.
To ponder and intensely evaluate a problem; to struggle to deal with.
senses.example: to grapple with one's conscience

senses.definition: To fasten, as with a grapple; to fix; to join indissolubly.
senses.example: The two crews grappled the ships together with heavy iron chains.

senses.definition: To climb (whether by means of a grapple and rope, or by hand, etc).
senses.example: The climbers grappled up the cliff face using ropes and iron hooks.

senses.definition: To use a grapple (for example to attempt to find, hook, and raise a net or cable).
senses.example: Divers grappled along the seabed trying to recover the lost telephone cable.

senses.definition: To hook and raise with a grapple.
senses.example: The crew grappled the sunken anchor from the harbor floor before dawn.

senses.definition: A close hand-to-hand struggle.
senses.example: The two wrestlers ended their brief grapple in the center of the ring.

senses.definition: The act of grappling.
senses.example: A sudden grapple left the thief pinned against the alley wall.

senses.definition: A tool with claws or hooks which is used to catch or hold something.
senses.example: He lowered a grapple over the side to snag the mooring line.

senses.definition: A grapnel (“type of anchor”).
senses.example: The small boat carried a grapple for anchoring in the quiet cove.

senses.definition: A combination of grape and apple flavors.
senses.example: The new soda has a grapple flavor that surprised everyone at the party.

senses.definition: A device consisting of iron claws, attached to the end of a rope, used for grasping and holding an enemy ship prior to boarding; a grappling iron.
senses.example: Pirates hurled a grapple across the rail to pull the merchant ship close.

core.definition: To struggle hard with a problem, or to physically seize and wrestle with someone or something, holding on firmly until you gain control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ple' is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so say it as 'GRAP-l' with the l sound carrying the last beat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it suggests effort, difficulty or a fight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grapple with (a problem) in news, work and everyday talk, as in 'grappling with a question'. Physically, it describes a struggle or wrestling. It is more vivid than 'deal with' and can sound dramatic if used for a small annoyance.

distinctions.note: Wrestle often means a physical struggle, while grapple can also describe a mental struggle with an idea.
Struggle is a broader word for difficulty, while grapple suggests holding on firmly to something hard.

examples.everyday: I'm still grappling with whether to take the new job, so I'll let you know next week.
examples.professional: Our team is grappling with how to handle the data backlog before the release.
examples.analytical: The author grapples with the tension between divine freedom and human responsibility throughout the essay.

nuance.analogy: It is like holding a rope in a tug of war: you keep a firm grip while the other side pulls, and you work to pull back.
nuance.etymology: From Middle French 'grappler', from 'grape' meaning hook, related to grapple as a grappling hook.
common_mistakes: Using 'grapple to' instead of 'grapple with' when the object is a problem.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'grap-PULL'.

grapple.etymology: From Middle English **grapplen* (“to seize, lay hold of”), from Old English **græpplian* (“to seize”), from Proto-Germanic **graipilōną*, **grabbalōną* (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʰrebʰ-* (“to take, seize, rake”), equivalent to *grab* + *le*.

senses.definition: An additional payment given freely as thanks for service.
senses.example: service gratuity

senses.definition: Euphemistic form of fee, in contexts where such additional payments have been made obligatory.
Euphemistic form of bribe.

core.definition: An extra amount of money given to a service worker, such as a waiter, as thanks for good service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable 'TOO'. The 'ui' is pronounced as a single 'oo-uh' glide, and the ending is a light 'tee'. Do not stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a polite, formal word for a tip, often used in hotels, cruises, or official contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, people usually say 'tip' rather than 'gratuity', which sounds formal or official. 'Gratuity' is common on hotel bills, cruise ships, and in service contracts, where it may be added automatically. Some businesses label a mandatory service charge as a gratuity, which some customers see as a fee rather than a voluntary tip.

distinctions.note: 'Tip' is the everyday word for money given to a server in a restaurant. 'Gratuity' is more formal and often appears on printed bills.
A 'service charge' is a fixed fee added by the business. A 'gratuity' is traditionally a voluntary extra payment, though it is sometimes added automatically.

examples.everyday: Do you want to leave a gratuity, or is the tip already included on the bill?
examples.professional: Our hotel group charges an automatic gratuity for banquet staff, and the amount is clearly listed on each invoice.
examples.analytical: The distinction between a gratuity and a mandatory fee matters legally, because one is voluntary while the other is part of the price.

nuance.analogy: A gratuity is like a thank-you card with money inside, a small extra beyond the price of the meal.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'gratuitas' or Middle French 'gratuité', from Latin 'gratuitus' (given freely).
common_mistakes: Using 'gratuity' in casual conversation where 'tip' is the normal American word.
Stressing the last syllable as 'gruh-too-ih-TEE'.

gratuity.etymology: From Middle French *gratuité* (from Old French *gratuite*) or directly from Medieval Latin *gratuitas* (“a free gift”), from Latin *gratuitus* (“freely given, free”); see *gratuitous*.

conversation.text: For groups of six or more, an 18% gratuity is added to the bill.
Check the receipt first; the gratuity might already be included.
Gratuity is not included, so remember to leave a tip.

senses.definition: Cautious; restrained.
senses.example: guarded outlook

senses.definition: A good outcome has fair odds of happening but close monitoring is important because odds of deterioration are not low.
senses.example: guarded prognosis

senses.definition: Watched over; supervised.
senses.example: The prisoner was guarded by two officers every time he left the courthouse.

senses.definition: Having a guard, e.g. a crossguard (on a sword), a faceguard (on a helmet), or a hatguard (on a chapeau).
senses.example: The museum displayed a guarded sword with an ornate crossguard and a brass hilt.

core.definition: Careful and reserved, not showing your real feelings or opinions openly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GAR, and the r is clearly American. The ending is two short syllables, 'did', with the second one reduced to a quick 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive, as in prudent or careful, or negative, as in cold or distant, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans describe people who hold back emotions, especially after being hurt, and speakers who are careful in a conversation. The phrase guarded optimism is common in news and business: cautiously hopeful. A natural reply when someone asks about a meeting is 'I'm cautiously optimistic,' while 'I'm guarded about it' signals reluctance.

distinctions.note: Cautious is about avoiding risk, while guarded is about holding back information or feelings.
Reserved describes a personality trait, while guarded often describes a response to a particular situation.
Wary means suspicious and alert, while guarded focuses on not revealing much.

examples.everyday: She was pretty guarded at first, but she opened up after a couple of drinks.
examples.professional: The CFO gave a guarded answer about the Q3 forecast, so we should confirm the numbers before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: Her guarded phrasing suggests she is protecting her position rather than stating a firm conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with the blinds half-drawn, a guarded person lets a little light in but shows little of the room.
nuance.etymology: From the verb guard, meaning to protect or keep safe, plus the past-participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Using guarded only in a negative sense; guarded optimism is positive.
Confusing guarded with careful; guarded means hiding feelings or information, not just being thorough.

senses.definition: In a tasteful, agreeable manner.

core.definition: A musical direction meaning to play with relish, flavor and enjoyment, with expressive and lively feeling.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -STOH-, as in Italian. Keep the middle s unvoiced, like the s in 'stop,' and don't turn the ending into 'so-so.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a manner of performance that is lively and expressive.
nuance.usage_note: Gustoso is an Italian musical term used in scores and by musicians, teachers and music critics. Americans rarely use it outside music. In everyday conversation you would say 'with gusto' or 'with relish.' The dictionary gloss about being tasteful is not the musical sense, so do not use it for food or behavior.

distinctions.note: Gusto is an English noun for enthusiasm, as in 'she cooked with gusto.' Gustoso is the Italian musical adverb meaning a similar spirit in performance.
Appassionato means passionately and intensely; gustoso means with lively relish and enjoyment, a lighter emotional color.

examples.everyday: My piano teacher said, 'Play it gustoso,' which means you should enjoy the tune and let it sparkle.
examples.professional: In the rehearsal notes, the conductor asked the strings to play the second theme gustoso, with more relish and less restraint.
examples.analytical: Musicologists note that gustoso markings often signal a shift from lyrical restraint to a more exuberant, flavorful articulation.

nuance.analogy: Gustoso is like saying a dish is served with real appetite, so the music itself seems to savor each note.
nuance.etymology: From Italian gustoso, 'tasty, pleasing,' from gusto, 'taste,' from Latin gustus.
common_mistakes: Using gustoso for food or tasteful clothes, which is not its meaning.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'GUS-to-so'.

senses.definition: A person who haggles.
(historical) A person who buys vegetables and other produce from farms and then sells them on in a different location; a person who transports farm goods.
senses.example: The haggler drove his wagon from farm to farm each morning, buying cabbages and potatoes to resell in town.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who bargains persistently with a seller, trying to lower the price of something they want to buy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Say the second syllable as a light, reduced 'ler,' with no extra vowel between the l and the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. A haggler can be admired as a shrewd shopper, but the word can suggest someone who is tiresome or stubborn in bargaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for people who negotiate prices at flea markets, garage sales, car lots, bazaars, and some international markets. In most American stores with fixed prices, bargaining is not expected. Calling someone a haggler usually means they are very good at getting a deal.

distinctions.note: A negotiator works toward a formal agreement on many terms, while a haggler focuses on the price, often through small, repeated offers.
Bargainer is a general term for someone who makes a deal, while haggler suggests persistent back-and-forth over money.

examples.everyday: My aunt is a fierce haggler at the flea market, and she has gotten rugs for a third of the asking price.
examples.professional: Our procurement lead is a tough haggler, so vendors usually lower their quotes before the contract even reaches legal.
examples.analytical: Economists often treat the haggler as an idealized agent in price bargaining, although real haggling depends heavily on social trust and norms.

nuance.analogy: A haggler is like a chess player who keeps testing a position until the other side finally gives ground.
nuance.etymology: Formed from haggle, a verb of uncertain origin, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using haggler for a person who pays a fixed price without bargaining, where shopper or customer is more accurate.
Mispronouncing haggler with an extra vowel, as 'HAG-uh-ler.'

senses.definition: The disease leprosy, caused by infection by Mycobacterium leprae.
senses.example: Her grandfather was treated for Hansen's disease at a federal hospital in Louisiana decades ago.

core.definition: The medical name for leprosy, a chronic bacterial infection that damages the skin and nerves.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -ZEEZ at the end, and the first word has a weaker stress with a reduced middle vowel. The 's' in 'disease' is pronounced like a z, and the name is said 'HAN-sunz', not 'han-SEN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to clinical; it is used to reduce the stigma that attaches to the word leprosy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans normally say leprosy in casual speech, but Hansen's disease is the preferred term in medicine, public health agencies and official writing, including the CDC. Using the term respects patients and avoids the stigma linked to leprosy. In a doctor's office, you might hear 'Hansen's disease is treated with a combination of antibiotics.'

distinctions.note: Same disease; leprosy is the everyday and historical term with heavy stigma, while Hansen's disease is the neutral medical term.
Both are caused by mycobacteria, but tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mainly affects the lungs.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the skin patches were not Hansen's disease, but she ran a test to be sure.
examples.professional: The public health report lists Hansen's disease cases by county and tracks how many patients complete treatment.
examples.analytical: Historians note that the stigma attached to leprosy shaped how societies isolated patients, and the term Hansen's disease became preferred partly to reduce that stigma.

nuance.etymology: Named after Gerhard Armauer Hansen, the Norwegian physician who identified Mycobacterium leprae in 1873.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'Hanson's disease' with an o
Stressing the first syllable as 'han-SEN'
Using leprosy casually when the neutral clinical term is Hansen's disease
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word tsara'at (צָרַעַת) and the Greek word lepra (λέπρα) in the Bible cover a broader range of skin diseases than modern Hansen's disease. Leviticus 13 describes how priests examined skin conditions and required the affected person to live outside the camp. In Mark 1:40-42, Jesus heals a man with leprosy, and in Luke 17:11-19 Jesus heals ten lepers, only one of whom returns to give thanks.

hansen's-disease.etymology: who in 1873 discovered the bacterium causing the disease.

senses.definition: Of material or fluid, solid and firm.
senses.example: This bread is so stale and hard, I can barely cut it.

senses.definition: Resistant to pressure; difficult to break, cut, or penetrate.
senses.example: This bread is so stale and hard, I can barely cut it.

senses.definition: Of drink or drugs, strong.
senses.example: He ordered a hard whiskey, neat, and the bartender poured it generously.

senses.definition: Of a normally nonalcoholic drink, containing alcohol.
senses.example: hard cider, hard lemonade, hard seltzer, hard soda

senses.definition: Very acidic or tannic.
senses.example: This young red wine tastes too hard, with harsh tannins that need a few years.

senses.definition: Of light, consisting of parallel rays, producing clearly defined shadows.
senses.example: The noon sun cast hard light across the parking lot, sharpening every shadow.

senses.definition: Of a personal or social setting, having a severe property; presenting difficulty.
senses.example: a hard problem; a hard question; a hard topic

senses.definition: Difficult or requiring a lot of effort to do, understand, experience, or deal with.
senses.example: a hard problem; a hard question; a hard topic

senses.definition: Demanding a lot of effort to endure.
senses.example: a hard life

senses.definition: Severe, harsh, unfriendly, brutal.
senses.example: a hard master; a hard heart; hard words; a hard character

senses.definition: Tough, muscular, badass.
senses.example: He thinks he's well hard.

senses.definition: Excellent, impressive.
senses.example: This song goes hard.

senses.definition: Unquestionable; unequivocal.
senses.example: hard evidence; a hard requirement

senses.definition: Of an intersection, having a comparatively larger or a ninety-degree angle.
senses.example: At the intersection, there are two roads going to the left. Take the hard left.

senses.definition: Sexually aroused; having an erect penis.
senses.example: I got so hard watching two hot girls wrestle each other on the beach.

senses.definition: Having muscles that are tightened as a result of intense, regular exercise.
senses.example: After months of training, her calves looked hard and defined under the gym lights.

senses.definition: Fortis.
senses.example: There is a hard c in "clock" and a soft c in "center".

senses.definition: Plosive.
senses.example: There is a hard c in "clock" and a soft c in "center".

senses.definition: Unvoiced.
senses.example: Hard k, t, s, ch, as distinguished from soft, g, d, z, j.

senses.definition: Of Slavic languages, velarized or plain, rather than palatalized.
senses.example: The letter ж (ž) in Russian is always hard.

senses.definition: Having a severe property; presenting a barrier to enjoyment.
senses.example: Organic chemistry is a hard course, and many students struggle through the first exam.

senses.definition: Rigid in the drawing or distribution of the figures; formal; lacking grace of composition.
senses.example: Critics called the painting hard and stiff, with figures arranged too formally.

senses.definition: Having disagreeable and abrupt contrasts in color or shading.
senses.example: The poster used hard reds and greens that clashed painfully against each other.

senses.definition: In a physical form, not digital.
senses.example: a soft or hard copy; a digital or hard archive

senses.definition: Using a manual or physical process, not by means of a software command.
senses.example: a hard reboot or reset

senses.definition: Far, extreme.
senses.example: hard right, hard left

senses.definition: Of silk, not having had the natural gum boiled off.
senses.example: The weaver chose hard silk for the lining because it held its crisp shape.

senses.definition: Of a market: having more demand than supply; being a seller's market.
senses.example: With so few homes listed, the housing market has turned hard for buyers.

senses.definition: Hardcore.
senses.example: She's a hard punk who never misses a late-night show downtown.

senses.definition: Of water, high in dissolved chemical salts, especially those of calcium.
senses.example: Our tap water is hard, so the kettle develops a white scale within a few months.

senses.definition: Of a ferromagnetic material, having the capability of being a permanent magnet by being a material with high magnetic coercivity (compare soft).
senses.example: Neodymium is a hard magnetic material, so it keeps its field long after magnetizing.

senses.definition: Of electromagnetic radiation, having a high energy (high frequency; short wavelength).
senses.example: hard X-rays

senses.definition: Hardened; having unusually strong defences.
senses.example: a hard site

senses.definition: (dated) Difficult to resist or control; powerful.
senses.example: 'That's a hard temptation,' Grandma said, eyeing the last slice of pie.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: With much force or effort.
senses.example: He hit the puck hard up the ice.

senses.definition: With difficulty.
senses.example: His degree was hard earned.

senses.definition: Compactly.
senses.example: The lake had finally frozen hard.

senses.definition: A tire whose compound is softer than superhards, and harder than mediums.
senses.example: He chose hards for the long stint because they would last the whole race.

senses.definition: Crack cocaine.
senses.example: Detectives found a few rocks of hard tucked under the seat during the traffic stop.

senses.definition: Hard labor.
senses.example: The prisoners were sentenced to three years' hard.

senses.definition: A firm or paved beach or slope convenient for hauling vessels out of the water.
senses.example: We pulled the dinghy up the hard before the tide came in.

core.definition: Difficult to do, understand or endure; requiring much effort.

pronunciation.tip: Make the r clear and finish with a firm d. Do not add a vowel after it, as in HAR-duh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be negative for a difficult situation and positive when praising effort, as in a hard worker.
nuance.usage_note: Hard is one of the most common words in American speech. Everyday uses include a hard day, a hard test or a hard decision. As an adverb, hard means with a lot of effort, as in work hard or think hard, and it is different from hardly, which means almost not.

distinctions.note: Difficult is the more neutral, general word, while hard often stresses physical effort or a strong challenge.
Hardly means almost not and is not the adverb form of hard, though learners often confuse them.
Solid describes firmness of material; hard can mean firm but also difficult or tough.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, it was a hard day at the office and the traffic was terrible.
examples.professional: This migration is hard because the legacy database has almost no documentation.
examples.analytical: Hard problems in philosophy are hard not because they are obscure but because every answer seems to create a new difficulty.

nuance.analogy: A hard question is like a steep hill: you can climb it, but every step takes real effort.
nuance.etymology: From Old English heard, meaning firm, strong or difficult.
common_mistakes: Using hard where hardly is needed: I hardly slept means almost not at all, not I hard slept
Mispronouncing it with an added vowel, as HAR-duh
Assuming hard as an adverb always means difficult; with work or try it means with effort

hard.etymology: From Middle English *hard*, from Old English *heard*, from **hard*, from Proto-Germanic **harduz*, from Proto-Indo-European, from **kret-* (“strong, powerful”).

senses.definition: In a hateful manner.

core.definition: In a way that expresses hatred or is full of spite, cruelty, or hostility toward someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllable to a weak 'fuh'. The 'tf' blends into one sound, so the word is 'HAYT-fuh-lee', not 'HAYT-ful-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The adverb describes speech or behavior that is spiteful, cruel, or deliberately hurtful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hatefully' mostly in writing or in serious discussions of speech and behavior, such as harassment, online abuse, or hostile remarks. In casual speech people more often say 'meanly' or 'spitefully'. It describes how someone acts, not how they feel inside, so 'she spoke hatefully' is common but 'she felt hatefully' is not.

distinctions.note: 'Maliciously' means with intent to cause harm, while 'hatefully' suggests the action is driven by hostility or hatred.
'Spitefully' is petty and pointed, while 'hatefully' is a stronger and more serious word for hostility.

examples.everyday: She talked about her ex-husband hatefully at dinner, and it made everyone uncomfortable.
examples.professional: The comment was posted anonymously and written hatefully, so HR escalated it immediately.
examples.analytical: The essay shows how a rhetorical move can be framed hatefully without using a single slur.

nuance.analogy: Acting hatefully is like leaving a sharp note on someone's car, where each word is chosen to hurt rather than to inform.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'hateful' (hate plus -ful) and the adverb suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'hatefully' to mean 'with great dislike' in a neutral sense, when it always implies hostility or cruelty.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'hayt-FUL-ly' instead of 'HAYT-fuh-lee'.

senses.definition: Infernal, related or similar to hell.
senses.example: The traffic on the interstate was hellish during the holiday weekend.

senses.definition: Causing great pain, discomfort or distress.
senses.example: I woke up from a hellish noise coming from the house next door.

core.definition: Extremely unpleasant, painful or difficult, as if it were a part of hell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEL. The ending 'ish' is a short 'ish', so avoid stretching it into 'eesh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something terrible, often with humor or exaggeration in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hellish in casual speech to describe awful weather, traffic, or a bad week, often with a bit of humor. It can also mean literally infernal in religious or literary writing. In a formal setting, horrific or excruciating may sound more appropriate.

distinctions.note: Infernal is more literal and formal, referring to hell or devils, while hellish is more colloquial and often used for everyday misery.
Awful is a general word for bad, while hellish suggests a stronger sense of suffering or intensity.

examples.everyday: The traffic on the freeway was hellish this afternoon, so I'm exhausted.
examples.professional: The migration over the weekend was hellish, and we spent two days fixing broken database links.
examples.analytical: Dante's depiction of hellish landscapes uses vivid imagery to make moral consequences visible to the reader.

nuance.analogy: A hellish day is like a sauna without a door: nothing relieves the pressure, and you cannot leave.
nuance.etymology: From hell, with the suffix -ish meaning like or characteristic of.
common_mistakes: Using hellish for mild inconvenience in formal writing, which sounds exaggerated.
Stressing the second syllable (hel-LISH).

senses.definition: Without protection or assistance.
senses.example: The fish flopped helplessly in the tiny remaining pool.

senses.definition: Without the ability to help oneself.
senses.example: The boy rolled on the floor laughing helplessly.

senses.definition: Without the ability to react actively.
senses.example: The spectators gaped helplessly as the balloon approached the power lines.

core.definition: In a way that shows you cannot protect yourself, act or change a situation, often with frustration or sadness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -less ending is weak, and the l in helpless is syllabic, so it sounds like 'hel-pluh-slee' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes vulnerability, distress or frustration, and can sound dramatic in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use helplessly to describe watching a bad situation without power to stop it, as in 'I watched helplessly as the pot boiled over.' It is also used humorously in phrases like 'helplessly in love'. It is common in stories, news and emotional conversation.

distinctions.note: Powerlessly stresses lacking authority or political power, while helplessly stresses a personal inability to act.
Hopelessly means without hope or beyond repair, and it is often used in phrases like 'hopelessly lost'.
Helpfully means in a way that gives aid, which is the opposite meaning, so do not confuse the two.

examples.everyday: I stood there helplessly while my toddler dumped cereal all over the floor.
examples.professional: Our team watched helplessly as the server crashed during the launch, since we had no backup plan.
examples.analytical: Many readers of Hume feel helplessly caught between reason and custom when they try to justify causal claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger in a car with no steering wheel: you can see the road but cannot turn.
nuance.etymology: From helpless (help plus -less) with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing helplessly (unable to act) with helpfully (in a helpful way), which has the opposite meaning.
Putting the stress on -less, as in 'help-LESS-lee'. The stress stays on HELP.

senses.definition: The practice of accumulating goods.
senses.example: Her grandfather's hoarding of old newspapers filled every room of the house by the time he died.

senses.definition: A good which is hoarded.
senses.example: Police found a hoarding of gasoline and canned food stashed behind the warehouse wall.

senses.definition: An anxiety disorder characterized by a compulsive need to accumulate goods and feelings of anxiety or discomfort about discarding such goods.
senses.example: My therapist said her hoarding disorder made it nearly impossible to throw away anything, even expired coupons.

senses.definition: (historical) A roofed wooden shield placed over the battlements of a castle and projecting from them.
senses.example: The defenders crouched beneath a wooden hoarding while arrows rattled harmlessly off the castle's parapet.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The act of collecting and storing large amounts of something, often beyond what is needed, sometimes out of fear that it will run out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounce the r, and keep the second syllable short and light. The final -ing is quick and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it describes excessive stockpiling or greed, and neutral in technical or economic discussion.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, hoarding describes people buying up toilet paper, water or medicine during a crisis, which people often criticize. In Britain, a hoarding is a wooden fence around a construction site or a billboard, but Americans call that a construction fence or billboard. Hoarding is a common word in news and in mental health talk, often as hoarding disorder.

distinctions.note: Stockpiling is planned and often considered responsible, such as keeping emergency supplies, while hoarding suggests excess and greed.
Saving means setting aside money or things for later use, while hoarding means keeping them out of reach or circulation, often to excess.

examples.everyday: People started hoarding toilet paper again, so the shelves were empty by noon.
examples.professional: Hoarding of inventory by one supplier distorted our quarterly forecast, so we adjusted the reorder points.
examples.analytical: Economists often treat hoarding as a rational response to uncertainty, though it can make shortages worse for everyone else.

nuance.analogy: Hoarding is like a bank vault that never opens, even when the money is needed by the community.
nuance.etymology: From the verb hoard, from Old English hord meaning treasure, with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using hoarding as a neutral word for careful saving, when Americans hear it as excessive.
Confusing the American meaning with the British meaning of a hoarding as a construction fence or billboard.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use a single word for hoarding, but the Greek verb thēsaurizō means to store up treasure. Matthew 6:19-21 contrasts storing up treasure on earth with storing up treasure in heaven. Luke 12:16-21, the parable of the rich fool, describes a man who builds bigger barns for his grain and is called foolish because he stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

senses.definition: The condition of being homogeneous: having uniformity of constituent content.

core.definition: The quality of being uniform in makeup or character; in statistics, equal variances across groups.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NEE, the fourth syllable. Say the middle syllables quickly with reduced vowels, and the final -ity is ih-tee, not ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts. It can sound negative in social discussions, suggesting a lack of diversity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use homogeneity in statistics, science, and in discussions of communities or markets. In statistics, a test of homogeneity checks whether groups come from the same population. In social talk, people may say 'lack of diversity' instead, which sounds less technical and more sensitive.

distinctions.note: Uniformity means sameness or consistency in general, while homogeneity specifically refers to similarity of composition or character across a whole group.
Homogenization is the process of making something uniform, while homogeneity is the resulting state.

examples.everyday: The town feels so homogeneous, but I think the new restaurants are bringing more variety.
examples.professional: Before we pool the survey results, we need to check the homogeneity of the regional samples.
examples.analytical: The assumption of homogeneity across cohorts is often violated in longitudinal studies, which can bias the conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Like a pitcher of milk that has been mixed so the cream does not separate: every spoonful tastes the same.
nuance.etymology: From Greek homogenēs (of the same kind), from homos (same) and genos (kind), with the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing homogeneity with homogenization, which is the process rather than the state.
Using homogeneity as a casual word for sameness in everyday talk, where similarity or uniformity fits better.

senses.definition: Sweetened, with, or as if with, honey.
Sugary, syrupy.
senses.example: She poured honeyed tea over the warm biscuits and sat by the window.

senses.definition: Dulcet or mellifluous.
senses.example: The preacher's honeyed voice soothed the restless congregation during the long benediction.

core.definition: Sweetened with honey, or sounding smooth and sweet like honey. Often describes pleasant voices or words that may be flattering.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ed reduces to a short 'id' sound. Do not stretch it into HUN-eed.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. Describing a voice as honeyed is positive, but honeyed words often suggest flattery or insincerity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use honeyed in writing, speeches and descriptions of voices, especially in literary or journalistic style. Honeyed words implies flattery that may not be sincere. In everyday speech people more often say sweet or smooth, though honeyed can describe a voice that is especially warm.

distinctions.note: Sugary often suggests excessive sweetness or sentimentality, while honeyed usually suggests a smooth, warm sweetness that can be pleasant.
Mellifluous is a more formal word for smooth, pleasing sound, mainly applied to voices and music, while honeyed can also suggest flattery.

examples.everyday: She has a honeyed voice that makes everyone want to keep listening to her stories.
examples.professional: The vendor's honeyed pitch sounded great, but we need the contract terms in writing before we commit.
examples.analytical: Writers from classical antiquity onward have warned that honeyed flattery can disguise a manipulator's real intentions.

nuance.analogy: Like a spoonful of honey: it goes down smoothly, but you may not notice what it is covering.
nuance.etymology: From honey, with the adjective ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Using honeyed only for food, when it is more often used to describe voices or speech.
Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable, as in HUN-eed.

senses.definition: A dangerous situation; trouble.
senses.example: Both students are in hot water from fighting.

senses.definition: Fierce criticism.
senses.example: The government's new proposal has landed them in hot water.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hot,‎ water.

core.definition: Trouble or a difficult situation, especially one that brings criticism, scolding or punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WA in water, with lighter stress on hot. The t in water is a flap, so it sounds like WAW-dur in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes trouble you have brought on yourself or a serious consequence to come.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use in hot water for a kid who breaks a rule, an employee who misses a deadline, or a public figure caught in a gaffe. It is mild and informal, weaker than in deep trouble. A natural reply is Oh no, what happened? or Did you get out of it?

distinctions.note: Trouble is general, while in hot water suggests you did something that will bring criticism or punishment.
In a jam means a difficult spot, often less serious and sometimes just inconvenient.

examples.everyday: Don't tell Mom I took the car, or I'll be in hot water.
examples.professional: If the vendor misses this deadline, we'll be in hot water with the client.
examples.analytical: Politicians who speak carelessly often land in hot water, since every remark becomes evidence against them.

nuance.analogy: Like being dropped into a pot that is already boiling: trouble arrives before you can climb out.
common_mistakes: Adding an article, as in in the hot water; the idiom is in hot water with no article
Using it for a literal sink or faucet situation; the idiom means trouble only

senses.definition: Affected by hunger; having the physical need for food.
senses.example: My kids go to bed hungry every night because I haven’t got much money for food.

senses.definition: Causing hunger.
senses.example: All this gardening is hungry work.

senses.definition: Eager; having an avid desire or appetite for something.
senses.example: young and hungry

senses.definition: Not rich or fertile; poor; barren; starved.
senses.example: a hungry soil

core.definition: Wanting or needing food, or having a strong desire for something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, HUNG. The ng sound is one nasal consonant, followed by a hard g, and the final -ry is a clear American 'ee' sound with a flapped vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an ordinary word for physical need, and it can be positive when describing eagerness or ambition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hungry constantly in everyday talk, such as 'Are you hungry?' or 'I'm starving.' Starving is more emphatic and informal. In a restaurant, a host might ask, 'Are you hungry?' A natural reply is 'Yes, I could eat something.' Hungry for something abstract, such as success, is also common.

distinctions.note: Starving is more intense and informal, often an exaggeration in everyday speech, while hungry is the normal neutral word.
Famished is stronger and more informal than hungry, suggesting that you are extremely hungry.

examples.everyday: Are you hungry? I can make us some sandwiches before the movie.
examples.professional: The team is hungry for a win, so let's set a tight timeline for the next sprint.
examples.analytical: The hungry heart in the psalm longs for God as the deer longs for flowing streams.

nuance.analogy: Being hungry is like a phone battery running low: the body is signaling that it needs fuel.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hungrig, from hunger.
common_mistakes: Using hungry as a verb: say 'I am hungry,' not 'I hungry.'
Pronouncing the g in a soft 'j' sound, as in 'HUN-jree.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, hunger often means physical need, and the Greek word peinao means to hunger. Matthew 5:6 says those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. Luke 1:53 says God fills the hungry with good things. Matthew 25:35 describes feeding the hungry as service to Christ.

hungry.etymology: From Middle English *hungry*, from Old English *hungriġ*, from **hungrug*, from Proto-Germanic **hungrugaz* (“hungry”); equivalent to *hunger* + *y*.

conversation.text: Are you hungry? I can make sandwiches.
I'm not very hungry; I had a big lunch.
Let's eat; the kids are hungry.

senses.definition: Relating to a nickname, usually indicating intimacy with the person.
senses.example: My mother used a hypocoristic pet name for me that nobody else dared repeat.

senses.definition: Relating to baby talk.
senses.example: The toddler's hypocoristic babbling about doggy and nana delighted the whole family.

senses.definition: A nickname, especially one indicating intimacy and formed through a shortening of the original name.
senses.example: Everyone at the office called him Bobby, a hypocoristic he never quite outgrew.

core.definition: Of or being a pet name, a shortened affectionate form of a name, such as 'Bobby' for Robert.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the RIS syllable. The first syllable is 'hy' and the rest are reduced vowels, so do not stress the 'puh' or 'kuh' parts.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in linguistic description, though the names themselves express affection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in linguistics and in discussions of name forms. In everyday speech, people say 'nickname' or 'pet name.' If you use hypocoristic in conversation, people may ask what it means, so explain that it describes an affectionate short form.

distinctions.note: Nickname is the everyday word for any informal name, while hypocoristic is a technical term for an affectionate shortened form.
A diminutive is often a suffix that makes a word smaller or cuter, while a hypocoristic can be a shortened name without any suffix.

examples.everyday: Her mom still calls her Katie, a hypocoristic of Katherine, even though she's thirty.
examples.professional: In the onboarding form, we store each user's hypocoristic name separately from the legal name.
examples.analytical: Hypocoristic forms show how languages signal intimacy by reshaping a name rather than simply using its formal version.

nuance.analogy: A hypocoristic name is like a favorite old sweater: it is a shorter, softer version of the same thing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hypokoristikos 'caressing, endearing', from hypokorizesthai 'to call by pet names'.
common_mistakes: Using hypocoristic as a casual synonym for any nickname, when it is a technical term.
Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

hypocoristic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ὑποκοριστικός*, from *ὑποκορίζομαι* (“to speak in the language of children”), from *ὑπό* (“below”) + *κορίζομαι* (“to act like a girl”), from *κόρη* (“girl”).

senses.definition: To render into, or regard as, a separate and distinct substance; to construe a contextually-subjective and complex abstraction, idea, or concept as a universal object without regard to nuance or change in character.
senses.example: Critics argue that the team hypostatizes customer satisfaction into a fixed metric, ignoring how it shifts.

senses.definition: To attribute actual or personal existence to.
senses.example: Some ancient peoples hypostatized the wind as a god with a will and a name.

core.definition: To treat an abstract idea as if it were a real, separate thing with its own independent existence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PAH. Pronounce the middle syllables quickly and lightly, with a reduced vowel in stuh, and avoid saying it as hy-po-STAT-ize.

nuance.connotation: Negative or critical in most uses, because it implies a mistake: treating something abstract as concrete.
nuance.usage_note: Philosophers and theologians use this word to criticize reasoning that turns a concept into a thing, such as treating 'the economy' as a single agent that decides things. Americans rarely use it in casual talk. In conversation you would more likely say 'treating X as if it were a real thing.'

distinctions.note: Reify is the more common term in sociology and philosophy and means the same basic error, while hypostatize carries a stronger classical philosophical flavor.
Personify means giving human qualities to a thing, such as 'Nature is cruel'; hypostatize means treating an abstraction as an independent entity.

examples.professional: Our model team kept hypostatizing 'user intent' as one fixed variable, so we rewrote the spec to treat it as something measured from behavior.
examples.analytical: To hypostatize a relational property is to mistake a pattern of interaction for an independent substance, and this error underlies much of the metaphysical confusion Hume exposed.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a rainbow a solid object because you can point at it, hypostatizing gives an abstraction a fixed body it does not have.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin hypostatizare, from Greek hypostasis, meaning substance or foundation, from hypo- under and histanai to stand.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with hypothesize, which means to propose a tentative explanation.
Stressing the wrong syllable as hy-po-STAT-ize; the stress is on PAH.

senses.definition: To be honest, frankly, honestly.
senses.example: I can't lie, I was hoping you wouldn't notice.

core.definition: Used to say you are being completely honest, even when the truth is a little embarrassing or unwelcome.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIE, the last word. In fast speech can't is often weak and the t is barely released, so it sounds close to 'eye kan-LIE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals candor and a bit of self-awareness, and often introduces a compliment or a confession.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this casually to admit a real opinion, such as 'The pizza was cold, but I can't lie, it was still great.' It is friendly and conversational, not formal. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I'll take it' or 'Ha, I appreciate the honesty.'

distinctions.note: 'To be honest' is more neutral and works in almost any setting, while 'I can't lie' is more playful and informal.
'Frankly' sounds more formal and direct and can seem blunt, while 'I can't lie' sounds warm and personal.

collocations: I can't lie, I was impressed
I can't lie, that's a great idea

examples.everyday: The pizza was a little cold, but I can't lie, it still tasted amazing.
examples.professional: The vendor's demo missed two requirements, and I can't lie, I'm worried about the timeline.
examples.analytical: The author's objection is clever, and I can't lie that it unsettles my confidence in the original premise.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend who tells you the truth about your haircut, even though you were hoping for a compliment.
common_mistakes: Taking it literally as an inability to lie; in conversation it means you are being honest.
Using it in formal writing, where 'to be honest' or 'frankly' fits better.

senses.definition: Asking to schedule a visit with a doctor or service.

core.definition: A polite phrase for asking to schedule a visit with a doctor, dentist or service provider.

pronunciation.respelling: ide like too mayk an uh-POYNT-muhnt
pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POINT in appointment, and the second syllable is reduced to 'uh'. The word an is usually reduced to 'uhn' before a vowel, linking into 'uh-nuh-POYNT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this when calling a doctor's office, dentist or salon, and the receptionist often asks what kind of visit you need. Common replies include 'It's a new patient visit' or 'I need a checkup.' In a service context, 'schedule an appointment' is equally common.

distinctions.vs: I'd like to book a time.
distinctions.note: Book is common for hotels, restaurants and flights; appointment is the standard word for medical and professional services.

examples.everyday: I'd like to make an appointment with Dr. Lee for next week if she has an opening.
examples.professional: I'd like to make an appointment to review the quarterly report with the finance team.
examples.analytical: To make an appointment at the clinic, a patient must provide insurance information and describe the reason for the visit.

nuance.analogy: Like reserving a seat at a crowded show so the time is yours alone.
common_mistakes: Saying 'do an appointment' instead of 'make an appointment', which is the correct collocation.
Using 'make a reservation' for a doctor, which sounds unnatural.

conversation.text: Hi, I'd like to make an appointment for a checkup.
I'd like to make an appointment with Dr. Lee sometime next week.

senses.definition: Used to indicate emphatic agreement.
senses.example: - Jack's put on a bit of weight recently.- I'll say!

core.definition: Used to strongly agree with something someone has just said.

pronunciation.tip: I'll is one syllable, pronounced like 'aisle', and it is a contraction of 'I will'. Stress SAY, and do not pronounce it as 'I will say' in full.

nuance.connotation: Positive and emphatic. It can sound warm and enthusiastic, but it may also be playful or sarcastic depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in casual talk after something impressive or intense: 'That concert was loud.' 'I'll say, my ears are still ringing.' It sounds a bit folksy or old-fashioned, like 'you bet.' A natural reply is 'Right?' or 'Totally.'

distinctions.note: 'You can say that again' is more emphatic and more informal, almost a stronger version of 'I'll say.'
'Absolutely' is neutral and widely used in workplaces, while 'I'll say' is more casual.
'For sure' is casual and widely used, but it agrees with a fact more than it shows strong emotional agreement.

examples.everyday: Wow, that concert was loud. I'll say, my ears are still ringing.
examples.professional: The quarterly numbers beat every forecast. I'll say, the team deserves real credit for that result.
examples.analytical: The model's accuracy on the minority group is remarkable, and I'll say it challenges the assumption that fairness requires trade-offs.

nuance.analogy: Like a loud 'yes!' that comes out before someone has finished the sentence.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I will say' in full, which sounds stiff in casual speech.
Missing the sarcasm when someone says it with a flat tone, which can mean the opposite of agreement.

senses.definition: That is, namely, in other words, that is to say.
senses.example: While the final episode was made, the show itself was immediately canceled after the penultimate episode i.e. the final episode never aired.

core.definition: Means 'that is' or 'in other words'; used mainly in writing to restate or clarify what was just said more precisely.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters, 'eye-EE', with stress on the second letter, and never read it as the Latin 'id est'. When speaking aloud, Americans usually say 'that is' or 'in other words' instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals a precise restatement, but in casual speech it can sound pedantic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use i.e. in academic papers, reports, technical documents and legal writing to restate something more precisely; use e.g. when you mean 'for example'. It's usually written with periods and placed in parentheses or after a comma. In speech, people say 'that is' or 'in other words', and saying 'eye-ee' aloud can sound like spelling out letters.

distinctions.note: Introduces examples, not a restatement: 'some fruit, e.g. apples' versus 'the red fruit, i.e. the apple'.
A spoken or written alternative that introduces a specific, named item or list.
Rare and mostly in older scholarly or legal writing, where it introduces a list or detail.

examples.everyday: We'll be there around seven, that is, if the traffic isn't terrible.
examples.professional: Use the rolling mean (i.e., the average of the last seven days) for the baseline in the dashboard.
examples.analytical: Kant's categorical imperative binds all rational agents, i.e., anyone capable of reasoning, not only members of a particular community.

nuance.analogy: Like a translator's footnote that restates the original phrase in plainer terms.
nuance.etymology: From Latin id est, 'that is'.
common_mistakes: Confusing i.e. with e.g.; i.e. restates, while e.g. gives examples.
Reading i.e. aloud as 'eye-eh' or 'ih-ee' instead of the letters 'eye-EE', or better, saying 'that is' in speech.

senses.definition: A thing which intensifies the appreciation of something already good, or the regretting of something already bad.
senses.example: We went out for dinner and dancing and the icing on the cake was when my boyfriend proposed to me as we danced.

core.definition: Something extra that makes an already good situation even better; in irony, something that makes a bad situation worse.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'cake', and 'the' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant. In casual speech, 'on the' often sounds like 'ahn-thuh', with the n linking smoothly into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Positive, meaning a welcome bonus. It can also be sarcastic when used ironically for bad news.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in everyday conversation, in emails, and in speeches to describe a bonus that makes a good experience even better. A natural reply is 'Oh, nice, that's the cherry on top,' or simply 'Ha, totally!' The ironic version, 'And then the flight was canceled. Icing on the cake,' is common in casual talk.

distinctions.note: The cherry on top is a similar, slightly more playful image for a small extra bonus, while icing on the cake can suggest a larger, more satisfying extra.
The last straw is a negative idiom for the final problem that makes a person give up, while icing on the cake is usually positive or ironic.

collocations: that's the icing on the cake
the icing on the cake for us
a bonus that's the icing on the cake
to be the icing on the cake

examples.everyday: We had a great week at the lake, and then the hotel upgraded us to a suite, which was the icing on the cake.
examples.professional: The launch beat every target, and the executive bonus was the icing on the cake for the whole team.
examples.analytical: For the reformers, the new tax credit was merely icing on the cake, since the core policy had already passed.

nuance.analogy: A dessert that is already sweet becomes even more pleasing when someone adds a decorative topping.
nuance.etymology: The literal sense is the sugar coating on a cake; the figurative idiom extends that image of a pleasant addition.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the icing of the cake' or 'icing above the cake'; the fixed phrase is 'icing on the cake'.
Using it for a bad event without irony; in sincere speech it describes something good.

senses.definition: In an idealistic manner.

core.definition: In a way that focuses on high principles or perfect outcomes, often without regard to practical limits.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the LIS syllable, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The -ally ending is pronounced as -ik-lee, with the vowel reduced to a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It can praise high standards or hint that someone is naive about reality, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word to describe someone who plans or argues in a principled way, often in politics, business or community projects. Saying a plan was 'idealistically' designed can suggest it ignores practical limits. It is more common in writing and news commentary than in quick conversation.

distinctions.note: Optimistically expresses hope about outcomes; idealistically emphasizes principle and high standards, sometimes beyond what is practical.
Realistically means considering practical limits; idealistically does the opposite, focusing on how things should be.

examples.everyday: My brother idealistically thinks we can all split the rent evenly, but nobody's income is the same.
examples.professional: The team idealistically assumed that every vendor would meet the deadline, so the timeline had no buffer.
examples.analytical: Rawls's theory is idealistically grounded in the notion of a fair original position, yet critics question its application to actual institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like drawing a map of a perfect city: the lines look elegant, but you still have to build on real ground.
nuance.etymology: From idealistic plus -ally; idealistic from ideal plus -istic.
common_mistakes: Confusing idealistically with ideally; idealistically describes an attitude, while ideally describes how things would be under perfect conditions.
Stressing the first syllable as in eye-DEE-uh-lis-tik-lee instead of placing the main stress on LIS.

senses.definition: Bearing full likeness by having precisely the same set of characteristics; indistinguishable.
senses.example: My car is identical with the one my mom has just bought.

senses.definition: Not different or other; not another or others; not different as regards self; selfsame; numerically identical.
senses.example: Both suspects gave identical statements to the police, word for word.

senses.definition: Exactly equivalent.
Of twins, sharing the same genetic code.
senses.example: The identical twins share the same DNA, so doctors compare their medical histories closely.

senses.definition: (rare) Approximating or approaching exact equivalence.
senses.example: The two paint colors looked nearly identical under the store's fluorescent lights.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Something which has exactly the same properties as something else.
senses.example: The forger produced an identical of the original painting, down to every brushstroke.

senses.definition: An identical twin.
senses.example: Their mother could never tell which of the identicals was which at family dinners.

senses.definition: A rhyme on the same syllable, such as "leave" and "believe".
senses.example: Many poets treat leave and believe as an identical rhyme, which some critics find too easy.

core.definition: Exactly the same in every way, so that two things cannot be told apart.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DEN. The first syllable is a reduced ih, not a long eye sound. The final syllable is a weak -kul with no separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a strong, precise word, and it is used positively when describing matching things or people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use identical in everyday speech about twins, outfits, forms and products, and in technical contexts for exact matches. It is strong, so it is less natural for things that are only similar. For near matches, say 'almost identical' or 'very similar.'
