pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEE. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so say 'kruh-tiv-nus' with the final -ness as a soft 'nus', not 'ness'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It suggests someone is hiding things in a way that makes others uneasy or suspicious, though it can be neutral when describing a private personality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use secretiveness to describe a person or organization that won't share information, such as a boss who hides plans or a family member who won't talk about money. It is more often said about a trait than about a single act; for a single act, people usually say secrecy or just that someone is being secretive. In casual talk, people often say 'why so secretive?' with a teasing tone.

distinctions.note: Secrecy is the condition of keeping things hidden, often as a policy or practice; secretiveness is a personal tendency or character trait.
Privacy is a right to keep personal matters to oneself and is usually neutral or positive, while secretiveness suggests something is being hidden and carries a suspicious tone.

examples.everyday: Her secretiveness about the surprise party drove everyone crazy.
examples.professional: The team's secretiveness about the new model made it hard for anyone else to review the code.
examples.analytical: Secretiveness in powerful institutions can protect their interests while steadily eroding public trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a closed door in a house with no visible reason for it, secretiveness makes people wonder what is on the other side.
nuance.etymology: From secretive, from Latin secretus, 'set apart, hidden', plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in 'sec-RE-tiveness'.
Confusing secretiveness with secrecy when describing a company policy; secrecy is usually the better word for an official practice.
Saying 'secretness', which is not a word.

senses.definition: The fact or process of securitizing assets; the conversion of loans into securities, usually in order to sell them on to other investors.
The act of convincing a relevant audience to treat a topic as a matter of security (regardless of whether it constitutes an actual threat), thus justifying the use of extraordinary measures.
senses.example: Critics warned that the government's securitization of climate policy would justify emergency powers without real debate.

core.definition: In finance, the process of turning loans or other assets into tradable securities that are sold to investors.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on -zay-, with a secondary stress on kyoor. The middle vowels are reduced, so the word sounds like 'sih-kyoor-uh-tuh-ZAY-shun' rather than four full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical.
nuance.usage_note: In American finance, securitization is common in banking and mortgage discussions, especially after the 2008 financial crisis. Americans rarely use it in casual talk. In security studies it means something different, so check the context.

distinctions.note: Securities are the financial instruments themselves; securitization is the process of creating them from assets.
Syndication means a group of banks sharing a loan; securitization converts loans into securities sold to investors.

examples.everyday: After the bank started selling its car loans to investors, my friend asked what securitization meant, and I said it was packaging loans into bonds.
examples.professional: Our risk team needs the securitization model updated so it accounts for borrower default rates in the new loan pool.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that securitization spread risk widely while also obscuring the quality of the underlying loans.

nuance.analogy: Securitization is like turning a box of individual loans into a single packaged product that many investors can buy.
nuance.etymology: From securitize, formed from security plus the suffix -ize, plus the noun ending -ation.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'security' in the everyday sense of safety.
Using it as a verb form; the verb is securitize.

senses.definition: Rule of a group of people by their own leaders as opposed to rule imposed by a foreign government or people.
senses.example: Britain resumed direct control of North Ireland after just nine weeks of self-rule.

core.definition: Government of a people or territory by its own leaders and laws, rather than by an outside power or foreign government.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on ROOL, with a light secondary stress on self. Use a long 'oo' sound, as in 'cool', not the short 'u' of 'rule' in 'run'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests independence and dignity, but it can be politically charged in disputes over sovereignty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in history, political science, and discussions of tribal sovereignty, territories or colonial independence. In everyday speech they more often say self-government or home rule. Saying self-rule at a barbecue would sound like a political lecture.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly identical, but self-government is the more common American term for a community running its own affairs.
Self-determination is the right of a people to choose their political status, while self-rule is the actual exercise of governing.
Independence means full separation from another state, while self-rule can exist inside a larger state, as with home rule.

examples.everyday: Some people on our street want more self-rule, so we can decide our own park rules without waiting on the county.
examples.professional: The partnership agreement grants the tribe significant self-rule over land use, but federal law still governs certain permits.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of democracy often argue that self-rule matters because it lets a people shape the laws that govern them.

nuance.analogy: Like a household that makes its own house rules instead of having a landlord set them for every room.
nuance.etymology: Compound of self and rule; rule comes from Latin regula, meaning straight stick or guideline.
common_mistakes: Using self-rule and self-determination as exact synonyms in formal writing, when they differ in meaning.
Saying self-ruling as the noun; the noun is self-rule.

senses.definition: In a selfish manner; with regard to private interest only or chiefly.
senses.example: She selfishly kept the last slice of pie for herself without asking anyone else.

core.definition: In a way that puts your own interests first, with little or no consideration for other people.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on SEL, and the -ly ending is an unstressed lee, giving three syllables. Keep the short i and the clean sh.

nuance.connotation: Negative; a moral criticism of how someone acted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use selfishly to criticize how someone acted, usually after the fact, as in He acted selfishly at the meeting. It is more common in writing and formal discussion than in casual talk, where people often say that was selfish instead. It sounds sharp in an argument, so use it carefully with friends.

distinctions.note: Unselfishly means generously putting others first, while selfishly is the opposite, putting your own interest first.
Selflessly is a warmer, more admiring word for giving without thought of reward, while selfishly is a criticism.

examples.everyday: I know you're tired, but you acted kind of selfishly when you took the last ride without checking with the group.
examples.professional: Our engineers shouldn't merge code selfishly, because it breaks the build for everyone who depends on the shared library.
examples.analytical: A person who acts selfishly may still be rational, but the ethical question is whether his reasons account for the interests of others.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds past a line of cars to get ahead, ignoring how it affects everyone else on the road.
nuance.etymology: From selfish plus -ly, the adverb suffix from Old English -lic.
common_mistakes: Using selfish as an adverb in speech, as in he did it selfish; use selfishly.
Using selfishly before a noun as an adjective, as in a selfishly man; use selfish there.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of seltzer water.

core.definition: Plain carbonated water with no added sugar or flavor, used for drinking or mixing with other drinks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The lt and ts blend into one quick sound, and the final syllable is a weak r-colored vowel, so do not say SELL-zer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday word for a simple product.
nuance.usage_note: In the Northeast, especially New York, people often say seltzer for unflavored sparkling water, and a seltzer bottle is a familiar object. In much of the rest of the country, people more often say sparkling water or club soda. Do not call sweet soft drinks seltzer; Americans call those soda.

distinctions.note: Club soda has added minerals for flavor, while seltzer is plain carbonated water.
Sparkling water is a broader term that may include mineral water from springs; seltzer is artificially carbonated water.
Tonic water contains sugar and quinine, which gives it a bitter taste; seltzer contains neither.

examples.everyday: Could I get a glass of seltzer with lime, please?
examples.professional: Please add a few cases of seltzer to the catering order for Thursday's offsite.
examples.analytical: Seltzer and club soda differ mainly in dissolved minerals, which changes both the taste and what the label may claim.

nuance.analogy: Seltzer is like a plain bedsheet: it carries the bubbles but adds nothing else, so it works with any drink.
nuance.etymology: Named after Selters, a town in Germany known for its mineral spring.
common_mistakes: Using seltzer to mean any soft drink or soda, which confuses Americans.
Pronouncing it with a z sound, as in SELL-zer, instead of the ts blend.

seltzer.etymology: A toponym from 1735–45 German *Selterser* (“of Selters”), after Selters, a village known for its carbonated mineral springs.

senses.definition: Search by meaning rather than exact keywords, usually using embeddings.
senses.example: Our new help desk tool uses semantic search, so customers find answers even with vague wording.

core.definition: Searching by meaning rather than exact keywords, usually by comparing vector embeddings of the query and documents.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'MAN' in 'semantic' and on 'SURCH' in 'search', with the r in 'search' clearly pronounced. Keep the 'ch' sound short and crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term that is also common in product descriptions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in data science, search engineering and product discussions. It contrasts with keyword search, which matches exact terms. In a meeting, a natural remark is 'We're moving the help center to semantic search so customers find answers even when they use different words.'

distinctions.note: Keyword search matches exact words; semantic search matches the meaning of the query, even with different wording.
Full-text search looks through all the text for matching strings; semantic search ranks results by conceptual similarity.

examples.everyday: I searched for 'cheap places to eat near the beach' and the app gave me good results, so it must use some kind of semantic search.
examples.professional: We added semantic search to the support portal, and the number of unresolved tickets dropped by about fifteen percent last month.
examples.analytical: Semantic search shifts the notion of relevance from lexical overlap to proximity in an embedding space, which raises new questions about what counts as a correct match.

nuance.analogy: Like asking a librarian for books about 'sad stories about the sea' rather than typing the exact title; the librarian understands what you mean.
nuance.etymology: Semantic from Greek semantikos, 'significant'; search from Old French cerchier, 'to seek'.
common_mistakes: Using 'semantic search' to mean any search engine; it specifically refers to meaning-based matching.
Stressing 'se-MAN-tik' with the stress on the wrong syllable.

conversation.text: Semantic search matches on meaning using embeddings rather than on exact keywords.
We combine keyword search with semantic search because product codes need exact matching.
With semantic search, typing "laptop won't charge" finds the article titled "Battery issues."

senses.definition: Of, or relating to old age.
senses.example: Her senile years were spent knitting by the window and reading old letters.

senses.definition: Exhibiting the deterioration in mind and body often accompanying old age; doddering.
senses.example: After the stroke, my uncle became senile and no longer recognized his own children.

senses.definition: (dated) A person who is senile.
senses.example: In the 1950s, the hospital ward housed a dozen senile who wandered the halls at night.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Showing the loss of memory, confusion, and mental decline that can come with very old age.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, with a long e as in 'see'. The second syllable rhymes with 'mile', so don't say 'sen-ile' with a short e.

nuance.connotation: Negative and often rude when applied to a person. It suggests that someone's mind has failed, so it can hurt or insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use senile in polite conversation; they say 'forgetful', 'confused', or 'has dementia' instead. Medical professionals now avoid the word in favor of dementia or cognitive decline. Using it as a joke about an older relative or coworker would likely offend people, and the noun form for a person is considered dated and unkind.

distinctions.note: Senior is a polite word for older people or for a higher rank, while senile is a negative term for mental decline.
Forgetful describes a mild lapse in memory and is neutral, while senile suggests serious and permanent mental decline.

examples.everyday: My grandfather's doctor said his memory problems come from a medication, not from being senile.
examples.professional: The insurance review excluded claims for conditions described as senile decline, because the policy now uses dementia codes.
examples.analytical: Older writers sometimes called aging minds senile, but modern neurology distinguishes normal aging from disease.

nuance.analogy: Like a lamp whose light dims and flickers, a senile mind loses clarity and steadiness over time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin senilis, of an old man, from senex, old.
common_mistakes: Confusing senile with senior, which is polite and neutral; calling an older person senile is rude.
Pronouncing the first syllable as a short e, which makes it sound like a different word.

senile.etymology: 1660s; borrowed from French *sénile*, from Middle French *senile*, from Old French *senile*, from Latin *senīlis* (“of or pertaining to old age”), from *senex* (“old man”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **sénos* (“old”).

senses.definition: (archaic) Seraphic: of or relating to a seraph or the seraphim; (by extension) pure and sublime.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Angelic, pure and sublime, like a seraph. This is an old form of seraphic and sounds archaic to most Americans.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -RAF-, the second syllable. The final syllables are weak, so the word ends in 'kul' rather than 'kal'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and elevated, suggesting holiness, purity and devotion. It can sound affectionate or exaggerated depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans now almost always say seraphic instead of seraphical. Seraphical appears mainly in older religious or literary writing, and using it in casual speech would sound dated. If you want a modern equivalent, say angelic or serene.

distinctions.note: Seraphic is the modern standard form, while seraphical is an archaic variant with the same meaning.
Angelic is common and everyday, while seraphical is more specific to the highest order of angels and sounds old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: In old novels the heroine is described as seraphical, but people today would just say angelic.
examples.professional: The editor cut seraphical from the manuscript because the word sounded too archaic for a modern readership.
examples.analytical: Medieval mystics often described divine love in seraphical terms, linking the burning ardor of the seraphim to the soul's longing for God.

nuance.analogy: Seraphical is like an old coat from a grandparent's closet: the meaning is still clear, but few people wear it today.
nuance.etymology: From seraph, from Hebrew sraphim, plural of saraph, meaning burning one, with the English adjectival ending -ical.
common_mistakes: Using seraphical in ordinary conversation, where seraphic or angelic is standard.
Spelling it seraphycal or using the wrong stress, placing it on the last syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the seraphim (singular seraph, Hebrew saraph, meaning burning one) are heavenly beings standing above the throne of the LORD in Isaiah 6:2, where the RSV names them seraphim. In Isaiah 6:6-7 one of them touches the prophet's lips with a live coal from the altar, which cleanses his guilt. Numbers 21:6 uses the same Hebrew root for the fiery serpents that bit the people in the wilderness, showing the word's basic sense of burning.

senses.definition: An act of being of assistance to someone.
senses.example: I say I did him a service by ending our relationship – now he can freely pursue his career.

senses.definition: The state of being subordinate to or employed by an individual or group.
senses.example: Lancelot was at the service of King Arthur.

senses.definition: Work as a member of the military.
senses.example: Thank you for your service.

senses.definition: The military.
senses.example: the service

senses.definition: The practice of providing assistance as economic activity.
senses.example: Hair care is a service industry.

senses.definition: Synonym of utility (“commodity provided on a continuous basis by a physical infrastructure network, such as electricity, water supply or sewerage”).
senses.example: Our apartment lost water service for six hours after the main broke.

senses.definition: A department in a company, organization, or institution.
senses.example: I work in the customer service department, answering billing questions all day.

senses.definition: A function that is provided by one program or machine for another.
senses.example: This machine provides the name service for the LAN.

senses.definition: A set of dishes or utensils.
senses.example: She brought out the silver tea service.

senses.definition: A religious rite or ritual.
senses.example: The funerary service was touching.

senses.definition: The serving, or delivery, of a summons or writ.
senses.example: The service happened yesterday.

senses.definition: A taxi shared among unrelated passengers, each of whom pays part of the fare; often, it has a fixed route between cities.
senses.example: We took a service from the airport to the border town for ten dollars each.

senses.definition: A musical composition for use in churches.
senses.example: The choir practiced Byrd's Great Service for the Sunday evensong.

senses.definition: Access to resources such as hotel rooms and Web-based videos without transfer of the resources' ownership.
senses.example: Her streaming service lets her watch films without owning the copies.

senses.definition: Service tree.
senses.example: The service tree in the churchyard blooms white every late spring.

senses.definition: The sorb; the fruit of this tree.
senses.example: Her jam recipe called for service, a tart fruit picked after the first frost.

senses.definition: The act of initially starting, or serving, the ball in play in tennis, volleyball, and other games.
senses.example: The player had four service faults in the set.

senses.definition: The materials used for serving a rope, etc. such as spun yarn and small lines.
senses.example: He bound the frayed rope with tight service of spun yarn before lowering it over the side.

senses.definition: To serve.
senses.example: They service the customer base.

senses.definition: To perform maintenance.
senses.example: He is going to service the car.

senses.definition: To supply (media outlets) with press releases etc.
senses.example: Our firm services media outlets, sending them press releases every morning.

senses.definition: To make a repayment or pay interest (on a debt).
senses.example: It continues to be laden with intense debt servicing costs.

senses.definition: To inseminate through sexual intercourse.
senses.example: The breeder serviced the mare twice before she was confirmed in foal.

senses.definition: To perform a sexual act upon.
senses.example: He serviced her several times a week.

senses.definition: To attack.
senses.example: to service a target

core.definition: Help or work done for someone, or a regular system that provides something useful to customers or the public, such as repairs or transportation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a short, reduced i, not ee or ay. End with the unvoiced s sound, not z, and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; good service is praised, and poor service is a common complaint. In formal contexts like military service or civil service it sounds dignified.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use service often in daily life, for example saying Thanks for the great service to a waiter, calling customer service for a store, or taking a car in for service. In restaurants, service also means how attentive and quick the staff are. As a verb, service is technical, so Americans say serve customers in everyday speech but may say service the car or service the equipment for maintenance.

distinctions.note: Help is any kind of assistance, while service usually means an organized or regular provision of work or support, often for pay.
Maintenance keeps something working over time, while service can mean a scheduled check, repair or task for a product or business.
Serve is the everyday verb for bringing food or helping someone, while service as a verb is mostly technical, for maintenance or sending media material.

examples.everyday: The service at that new coffee shop is really friendly, and they remember our names.
examples.professional: Our customer service team will handle refund requests within two business days.
examples.analytical: Civil service in democratic states is often justified as a duty owed to citizens rather than a private favor.

nuance.analogy: Service is like a well-run kitchen: nobody notices it when it works well, but everyone notices when it fails.
nuance.etymology: From Latin servitium, from servus meaning slave, through Old French service.
common_mistakes: Using service as a verb in everyday talk, as in service the table, when serve the table is the normal phrase.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a long i or ee sound, making it sound like ser-VICE or SER-veess.
Using service as a plural count noun in general sense, such as many services of help, when service is usually uncountable for general help.

senses.definition: A restraint fitted over a human or animal appendage, such as an ankle, finger, or wrist, normally used in a pair joined by a chain.
senses.example: The prisoner lay in shackles in his gloomy cell.

senses.definition: A U-shaped piece of metal secured with a bolt or pin across the ends, or a hinged metal loop secured with a quick-release locking pin mechanism, used for attaching things together while allowing for some degree of movement; a clevis.
senses.example: The engineer attached the lifting shackle to the chain before the crane raised the engine block.

senses.definition: Part of a padlock that consists of a loop of metal (round or square in cross section) that encompasses what is being secured by the lock.
senses.example: The padlock's shackle was cut clean through with bolt cutters in under a minute.

senses.definition: Synonym of hobble or hopple (“a short strap tied between the legs of a horse, allowing it to wander a short distance but not to run off”).
senses.example: The farmer tied a shackle around the mare's front legs so she could graze but not wander.

senses.definition: A link for connecting railroad cars; a draglink, drawbar, or drawlink.
senses.example: The switchman dropped the shackle between the boxcars, linking the freight cars for the trip.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of shackle-bone (“wristbone, carpal; wrist”).
A restraint on one's action, activity, or progress.
senses.example: Strict budget rules were a shackle on the department's ability to hire new analysts.

senses.definition: A person who is idle or lazy; an idler.
senses.example: Grandpa called my cousin a shackle because he spent every afternoon napping on the porch.

senses.definition: A dice game; also, an event at which tickets are sold for chances to be drawn to win prizes; a raffle.
senses.example: The church hall hosted a shackle last night, selling chances on a quilt and a ham.

senses.definition: A hook, ring, or other device for connecting, holding, lifting, etc. specifically, a small incomplete ring secured with a bolt across the ends, used to connect lengths of cable or chain together, or to keep a porthole closed.
senses.example: Use a stainless shackle to hold the cargo net, and check the bolt before each trip.

senses.definition: A length of cable or chain equal to 12½ fathoms (75 feet or about 22.9 meters), or later to 15 fathoms (90 feet or about 27.4 meters).
senses.example: The old captain measured the anchor rode in shackles, each roughly seventy-five feet long.

senses.definition: To place (a person or animal) in shackles (noun etymology 1 sense 1); to immobilize or restrain using shackles.
senses.example: This law would effectively shackle its opposition.

senses.definition: To connect or couple (something) to another thing using a shackle (noun etymology 1 sense 1.1.1, etymology 1 sense 1.1.3, etc.).
senses.example: Before the tow began, the crew shackled the trailer to the truck's heavy-duty hitch.

senses.definition: To provide (something) with a shackle.
senses.example: The rigger shackled each corner of the load before the crane lifted it.

senses.definition: To inhibit or restrain the ability, action, activity, or progress of (someone or something); to render (someone or something) incapable or ineffectual.
senses.example: This law would effectively shackle its opposition.

senses.definition: Of two things: to connect or couple together.
senses.example: The two cargo containers shackled together during the storm and rode out the waves.

senses.definition: To rattle or shake (something).
senses.example: The ghost in the attic shackled chains all night, keeping the children awake.

senses.definition: To put (something) into disorder; specifically, to cause (standing stalks of corn) to fall over.
senses.example: The windstorm shackled the cornfield, leaving stalks bent flat across the rows.

senses.definition: Often followed by about: to be idle or lazy; to avoid work.
senses.example: My brother shackled about all summer instead of finding a job.

core.definition: A metal ring or cuff fastened around a person's wrist or ankle to restrain them, usually in a pair joined by a chain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SHAK. The second syllable is a weak unstressed l, so do not add a separate vowel between k and l.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests captivity, punishment, or the loss of freedom.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shackle in news, history, legal, and literary contexts, such as slavery or prison. In everyday speech people more often say chains or cuffs. The verb to shackle means to restrain someone with shackles, and it can also be used figuratively for a limitation, as in shackled by debt.

distinctions.note: A chain is a flexible series of links, while a shackle is a restraint fitted around a limb.
Handcuffs are used by police for temporary restraint, while shackles are heavier and usually attached to a chain or to a fixed object.

examples.everyday: The old movie showed prisoners in shackles walking along the road.
examples.professional: We removed the legacy dependencies that shackled the team to a single vendor.
examples.analytical: The prophet describes the people as shackled by their own injustice, unable to move toward the covenant.

nuance.analogy: Like a pair of heavy bracelets locked around the ankles, limiting each step.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sceacul, a fetter, related to the noun shackle and to the verb meaning to fasten.
common_mistakes: Saying SHAK-ul with a vowel between the k and l.
Using shackle as an everyday word for a handcuff or cuff in casual conversation.
nuance.biblical_note: Shackles appear in the RSV in Psalm 149:8, where kings are bound with chains and nobles with fetters of iron. In Acts 12:6 Peter sleeps bound with two chains between two soldiers, and in Judges 16:21 Samson is bound with bronze fetters by the Philistines.

shackle.etymology: From Middle English *shakel*, *schakkyl*, *schakle* (“a fetter, shackle; coupling used to connect a plough or wagon to a draft chain”), from Old English *sċacul*, *sċeacel*, *sċeacul* (“fetter, shackle”), from **skakul*, from Proto-Germanic **skakulaz*…

core.definition: A man named in the Bible, including a Reubenite spy sent into Canaan (Numbers 13:4) and a son of David (2 Samuel 5:14).

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MOO. The final syllable is a weak 'uh', and the vowels should not be separated into extra syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a proper name with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Shammua is a biblical name used mainly in Bible study or Scripture reading. Several men share the name, so context matters. Americans say it smoothly, with the stress on the middle syllable.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school we read about Shammua, one of the spies who went into the land of Canaan.
examples.professional: For the study guide, list each man named Shammua separately, because the name refers to more than one person.
examples.analytical: The name Shammua appears in Numbers 13:4 for a Reubenite spy, in 2 Samuel 5:14 for a son of David, and in Nehemiah 12:18 for a priest.

nuance.analogy: Shammua is like a common family name that several people in one story share.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SHAM-oo-uh'.
Assuming all men named Shammua are the same person.
nuance.biblical_note: Shammua (Hebrew Shammua, שַׁמּוּעַ) is the name of several men in Scripture. In Numbers 13:4 he is the Reubenite spy sent by Moses with the others to explore Canaan, and in 2 Samuel 5:14 he is a son of David born in Jerusalem. Nehemiah 12:18 names a priest called Shammua in the days of Joiakim.

senses.definition: Any of the long-winged pelagic seabirds of the family Procellariidae in genera Puffinus, Ardenna, and Calonectris, that breed on islands and coastal cliffs.
senses.example: Thousands of sooty shearwaters returned to the island colony each spring to nest.

senses.definition: Any of the entire family Procellariidae, including certain of the petrels.
senses.example: Ornithologists grouped the shearwater with several petrels in the same family.

core.definition: A long-winged seabird that spends most of its life over the open ocean and comes to land mainly to nest on islands or coastal cliffs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHEAR, and the second syllable 'wa' is weaker than it looks. The final -er is a relaxed American 'ur' with no separate 'r' sound pushed out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise term used by birders, ornithologists, and naturalists.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shearwater mainly in birdwatching, ecology, and nature writing, and most people will recognize it only in those settings. In casual talk you might say 'a seabird' or name the species, such as 'a Manx shearwater.' Birders often use the word in trip reports and field guides.

distinctions.note: Shearwaters and petrels both belong to the family Procellariidae, but shearwaters have a more slender bill and fly low over waves with stiff, gliding wingbeats.
A puffin is a stocky, brightly billed seabird in a different family, Alcidae, and it is far more recognizable to the public.

examples.everyday: We took the boat out to see the shearwaters coming back to the island at dusk.
examples.professional: The coastal monitoring report counts shearwater nesting burrows on each of the three islands.
examples.analytical: The shearwater's life at sea, returning only to land to breed, shows how a seabird can be almost entirely separate from the coast it depends on.

nuance.analogy: A shearwater is like a commuter who spends the workday far from home and comes back only at night to raise the family.
nuance.etymology: From shear (to cut) and water, because the bird's wingtips seem to skim the surface of the sea.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'shear-WAH-ter.'
Confusing it with 'shear water', as in water cut by a boat, which is a different phrase.

senses.definition: To furnish (a place) with shelves; especially, to furnish (a library, etc.) with bookshelves.
senses.example: to shelve a closet or a library

senses.definition: To place (something) on a shelf; especially, to place or arrange (books) on a bookshelf.
senses.example: The library needs volunteers to help shelve books.

senses.definition: To place (something) in a certain location, as if on a shelf.
senses.example: Please shelve the returned books in alphabetical order by author.

senses.definition: To take (drugs) by anal or vaginal insertion.
senses.example: The doctor explained how to shelve the suppository and avoid discomfort.

senses.definition: To set aside (something), as if on a shelf.
To postpone or put aside, or entirely cease dealing with (a matter for discussion, a project, etc.).
To remove (someone) from active service.
senses.example: The airline will shelve the older jets once the new fleet arrives next year.

senses.definition: To extend via a series of projecting shelves.
senses.example: The cliff shelves gradually toward the river, forming wide ledges.

senses.definition: Of land or a surface: to incline, to slope.
senses.example: The ground shelves down sharply behind the barn toward the creek.

core.definition: To put a plan or project aside and stop working on it for now, often indefinitely.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short e as in 'bed' and end with a voiced v, not the f of 'shelf'. There is only one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests postponing or dropping something, usually without a firm decision to cancel it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'shelve' in meetings and business talk to mean delaying a project, as in 'Leadership shelved the proposal.' It implies the idea may return later, unlike 'scrap' or 'cancel,' which are final. A natural reply when someone says a plan was shelved is 'Do you know when it might come back?'

distinctions.note: Postpone means to move something to a specific later time, while shelve often means setting it aside with no firm date.
Scrap means to cancel something completely, whereas shelve keeps the idea alive for possible future use.

examples.everyday: The rain ruined our picnic, so we shelved the camping trip until the weather improves.
examples.professional: Leadership decided to shelve the database migration until the security audit is finished.
examples.analytical: Many reforms are shelved not because they fail but because they become politically inconvenient.

nuance.analogy: Shelving a project is like putting a book back on the shelf without throwing it away, so it can be picked up later.
nuance.etymology: From shelf; the verb meant to place something on a shelf, and the figurative sense of setting aside developed later.
common_mistakes: Spelling or pronouncing it as 'shelf' with an f at the end.
Using 'shelve' to mean permanently throwing something away, when 'scrap' or 'cancel' is the correct word.

shelve.etymology: The verb is a, the plural of *shelf* (“flat, rigid structure, fixed at right angles to a wall or forming a part of a cabinet, desk, etc. and used to display, store, or support objects”).

senses.definition: In a shoddy manner; lacking quality and done poorly, usually in a cheap and low quality way.
senses.example: The contractor had shoddily patched the roof, and it leaked after the first heavy rain.

core.definition: In a poor, careless way, producing something of low quality that is cheap and badly made.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The double d is one clear d sound, and the final -ily is a short ee sound. Do not confuse the first vowel with the one in 'shade.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes poor quality or careless workmanship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shoddily for construction, repairs, products, and service, as in 'The roof was shoddily installed.' It is a judgment, so use it carefully when speaking to the person who did the work. In a workplace, 'poorly' or 'carelessly' can sound less harsh.

distinctions.note: Carelessly focuses on a lack of attention, while shoddily focuses on the poor quality of the finished product.
Cheaply refers to cost or price, while shoddily refers to quality and workmanship.
Sloppily is informal and suggests messiness, while shoddily suggests poor construction or craftsmanship.

examples.everyday: The contractor patched the fence so shoddily that it fell over in the first storm.
examples.professional: The vendor delivered the server racks shoddily, so we spent two days re-cabling them.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the regime built its institutions shoddily, so they collapsed under the first real pressure.

nuance.analogy: A shoddily built bridge is like a house of cards: it looks fine until the first real weight arrives.
nuance.etymology: From shoddy (adjective) plus -ly; the origin of shoddy is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing shoddily with shabbily, which describes worn appearance or unfair treatment.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: Of poor quality or construction.
senses.example: Do not settle for shoddy knives if you are serious about cooking.

senses.definition: Poor; low.
senses.example: Do not settle for shoddy quality in your kitchen knives.

senses.definition: (dated) Pretentious, sham, counterfeit.
senses.example: The baron's shoddy manners fooled no one at the ball, though he wore the finest silk.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) Ambitious by reason of newly-acquired wealth; nouveau riche.
senses.example: The shoddy newcomer flaunted his wealth, buying a yacht he could not sail.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A low-grade cloth made from by-products of wool processing, or from recycled wool.
senses.example: The mill sold coats lined with shoddy, a cheap fabric that kept the rain out poorly.

senses.definition: Vulgar pretense or sham.
senses.example: His fine manners were pure shoddy, and everyone at the dinner could tell.

senses.definition: (dated) Worthless goods.
senses.example: The street vendor sold shoddy that fell apart before we got home.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Of poor quality, badly made or carelessly done, often while looking better than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The vowel is the open 'ah' sound, and the final 'y' is a light 'ee'. Do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes quality or behavior and suggests cheapness or dishonesty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'shoddy' for products, work, or service that is badly made, such as a 'shoddy repair' or 'shoddy workmanship.' It is a strong criticism, so use it with care about people's work. Among professionals it often describes sloppy analysis or documentation.

distinctions.note: 'Cheap' can mean low price, while 'shoddy' describes poor quality or construction, regardless of price.
'Flimsy' describes something that is physically weak or thin; 'shoddy' covers poor workmanship in general.

examples.everyday: The contractor did a shoddy job on the fence, and it already leans.
examples.professional: The vendor's shoddy documentation made the integration nearly impossible to debug.
examples.analytical: The argument is shoddy because it relies on a sample that cannot support its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a cheap sweater that looks fine on the hanger but unravels after one wash.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with stress on the second syllable.
Confusing it with 'shabby,' which more often describes worn appearance.

shoddy.etymology: *, but possibly from *shoad* (“loose stone and rubble; fragments”), equivalent to *shoad* + *y*; or possibly from the Arabic word for reuse.

senses.definition: One who fishes for or catches shrimp.
A boat used in fishing for shrimp.

core.definition: A person who fishes for shrimp, or a boat used to catch shrimp.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SHRIMP. The final -er is a reduced, rhotic r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce it as a full ehr.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it refers to a working person or vessel in the seafood industry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shrimper especially in the Gulf Coast and southern Atlantic states, where shrimping is an important industry. You may hear 'shrimp boat' more often than 'shrimper' for the vessel. A shrimper may be an independent fisher or work on a larger crew. In conversation, people often say 'he's a shrimper' or 'she runs a shrimp boat.'

distinctions.note: Fisherman is general and includes any fishing; shrimper refers specifically to those who catch shrimp.
Shrimper usually refers to the person, while shrimp boat specifically refers to the vessel used to catch shrimp.
A trawler is any boat that drags a net; a shrimper is a fisher or boat specifically for shrimp.

examples.everyday: My uncle worked as a shrimper in the Gulf for thirty years before he retired.
examples.professional: The shrimper's cooperative now requires traceability for every catch sold to restaurants.
examples.analytical: The shrimper's economic dependence on seasonal catch illustrates the vulnerability of coastal labor to market prices.

nuance.analogy: A shrimper is like a farmer working the sea, going out at dawn to bring home a harvest from the water.
nuance.etymology: From shrimp (noun) plus the agentive suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using shrimper for any fishing boat; it refers to shrimp fishing specifically.
Saying shrimp boater or shrimp fisher; the standard word is shrimper.

senses.definition: One who signs.
senses.example: John Hancock is a famous signer of the Declaration of Independence.

senses.definition: One who signs their name (applies their signature to something).
senses.example: John Hancock is a famous signer of the Declaration of Independence.

senses.definition: One who uses sign language.
senses.example: Among the hundreds of signers at the conference, most were native signers.

senses.definition: One who signs up another.
senses.example: The most prolific signers were to be amply rewarded by the sales-bonus structure.

core.definition: A person who signs a document, petition or contract, or a person who communicates in sign language.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SY. The vowel is a long i like sign, and the ending -er is a reduced American r-sound, so the word does not sound like singer.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role or action without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use signer for a person who signed a document, such as a petition or a lease, and in the Deaf community it describes a person who uses American Sign Language. In formal contracts people often prefer signatory. When speaking about sign language, Americans say a Deaf signer or a fluent signer, and hearing people usually say interpreter for someone who converts between languages.

distinctions.note: Signatory is a formal term for a party bound by an agreement, while signer is a general term for anyone who signs something.
A signer uses sign language directly, while an interpreter converts speech or text into sign language or the reverse.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a fluent signer, so she chats with her deaf brother every morning.
examples.professional: The conference provides a qualified signer for every session so that deaf attendees can follow along.
examples.analytical: The petition's signers represent a broad cross-section of the community, which strengthens its claim to legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: A signer is like a pen-pal who writes their name at the bottom of a letter: the signature makes the message personal and traceable to them.
nuance.etymology: From sign (verb) plus the agent suffix -er, from Latin signare 'to mark'.
common_mistakes: Confusing signer with singer, which is pronounced SING-er, because the spellings look similar.
Using signer as a formal term for a party bound by a treaty, where signatory is the standard word.

senses.definition: The property of being silky.
senses.example: The silkiness of the cashmere scarf made it my favorite thing to wear in winter.

core.definition: The quality of being smooth, soft, and glossy, like silk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SIL, and the 'ee' in the middle is a clear long vowel. The final '-ness' is a weak syllable, so say it as 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests smoothness and luxury in products, food, or voices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'silkiness' to describe hair, skin, sauces, fabrics, or a smooth voice, especially in beauty and food reviews. It is more descriptive than 'smoothness' because it adds a feeling of softness and shine. People rarely use it for character, except in a pleasant, figurative sense.

distinctions.note: Smoothness refers to the absence of roughness, while silkiness adds a soft, luxurious feel and often a slight gleam.
Softness describes how something yields under pressure, while silkiness describes a smooth, fine texture that slides against the skin.

examples.everyday: I love the silkiness this conditioner leaves in my hair.
examples.professional: The product team wants to measure silkiness with a texture panel rather than a sensor, since customers judge it by touch.
examples.analytical: Critics who praise the silkiness of the prose often reveal more about their taste than about the craft itself.

nuance.analogy: Silkiness is like water running smoothly over your hand: no catch, no roughness, just a soft flow.
nuance.etymology: From silk plus the noun suffix -iness, formed from the adjective silky.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'silkyness' by keeping the y from 'silky' instead of changing it to i before -ness.
Stressing the last syllable instead of SIL-kee-nus.

core.definition: In the Bible, a name shared by several men, most famously a son of Jacob and a righteous man who blessed the infant Jesus in the Temple. Americans say it as a name, not as an everyday word.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the last syllable is a reduced vowel, not a full 'on' sound. Many learners add an extra syllable or stress the second part, so keep it to three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a proper name with no emotional charge
nuance.usage_note: Simeon is mainly a biblical and religious name in American life, used in church, Bible study and sermons. Americans rarely use it in casual conversation except as a first name, which is less common today than Simon.

distinctions.note: Simon is the more common English form of the same Hebrew name, and it is the form used for Simon Peter; Simeon is the form used for Jacob's son and for the old man in Luke 2.

examples.everyday: My grandfather's middle name is Simeon, after a great-uncle.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Simeon appears as the example of waiting faithfully for God's promise.
examples.analytical: Luke presents Simeon as a model of the faithful Israelite who waits for the consolation of Israel and recognizes the Messiah in the infant Jesus.

nuance.analogy: Like a name that appears in the family tree of a Bible, Simeon is a figure you meet in more than one story, each with a different role.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shim'on, probably meaning 'hearing' or 'one who hears'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (sim-EE-on)
Pronouncing it like 'Simian' with an 'ay' vowel
Confusing Simeon with Simon, the name of Peter
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Shim'on (from shama, 'to hear'), Greek Symeon. Genesis 29:33 explains that Leah named her second son Simeon because the LORD heard that she was unloved; Genesis 42:24 has Joseph hold Simeon as hostage in Egypt; Luke 2:25-35 describes the righteous man Simeon who waited in the Temple and blessed the infant Jesus. Acts 15:14 uses the Greek form Symeon for Peter.

senses.definition: Lacking subtlety or sophistication.
Lacking mental capacity; feeble-minded.

core.definition: Overly simple in thinking; lacking subtlety or sophistication, or, of a person, lacking good mental capacity.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'MINE', and 'simple' is weak with a syllabic 'l'. The final '-minded' ends in a reduced 'id', not 'mined'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, and insulting when applied to people. When applied to ideas or arguments, it means they are too basic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'simple-minded' to criticize an argument, policy, or view that ignores important complexity ('a simple-minded solution'). When applied to a person, it is rude and suggests low intelligence, so avoid it in polite conversation. It is common in opinion writing and everyday criticism.

distinctions.note: Simplistic is more formal and academic, describing an analysis that oversimplifies a complex issue; simple-minded is more informal and can insult a person.
Naive means trusting and inexperienced; simple-minded suggests limited thinking or intelligence.
Simple is a neutral word for lacking complexity; simple-minded adds a critical judgment about thinking.

examples.everyday: That's a pretty simple-minded way to look at it, don't you think?
examples.professional: The proposal rests on a simple-minded assumption that users will read every warning message.
examples.analytical: Simple-minded accounts of moral failure ignore the social forces that shape the choices people make.

nuance.analogy: A simple-minded plan is like a map with only one road drawn on it, ignoring every alternative.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'simple' (from Latin simplex) and 'minded', from Old English gemynd, 'mind'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral description of a person; it is an insult.
Pronouncing 'minded' as 'mined' with a long 'i' and a full final vowel.
Using it where 'simplistic' would be more precise in academic writing.

senses.definition: A generalization of a triangle or tetrahedron to an arbitrary dimension; more accurately, the convex hull of n+1 affinely independent points in n-dimensional space.
A word which is not compound and contains no derivational affixes (inflectional affixes are usually disregarded); a monomorphemic word.
senses.example: The word weak is a simplex. Its derivative weaken is not.

senses.definition: An apartment (or, sometimes, another type of property) having only one floor or story; a single-story property.
senses.example: We rented a simplex on the edge of town, with a small yard and no stairs.

senses.definition: Of a circuit or device: involving signals which travel in one direction at a time; unidirectional.
senses.example: The amplifier uses a simplex circuit, so signals travel in only one direction at a time.

senses.definition: Of a polyploid organism: having one dominant allele at a given locus on all homologous chromosomes.
senses.example: The polyploid strain was simplex at the locus, with one dominant allele on every homologous chromosome.

senses.definition: Synonym of heterozygous (“of an organism: having two different alleles in a given gene”).
senses.example: In the genetics lab, the seedlings were simplex for the trait, carrying two different alleles each.

senses.definition: Of a word: having no (derivational) affixes; simple, monomorphemic, uncompounded.
senses.example: Linguists note that the word cat is simplex, with no affixes or compounding.

senses.definition: Of an apartment (or, sometimes, another type of property): having only one floor or story; single-story.
senses.example: Our new apartment is a simplex, so every room sits on the same floor.

senses.definition: (dated) Having a single structure; not composite or complex; undivided, unitary.
senses.example: The engineers preferred a simplex design, since one structure handled every task.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) Of an eye: (supposedly) having pigment on only the posterior surface of the iris and not the anterior surface, and thus appearing blue; this was later found to be inaccurate, as eye color is due to the amount of pigment in the anterior surface of the iris; also, of eye pigmentation: present only on the posterior surface of the iris; and of a person: having eyes with this form of pigmentation.
senses.example: Nineteenth-century physicians wrongly described his eyes as simplex, believing they looked blue for that reason.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: In mathematics, the simplest convex shape of a given dimension, such as a line segment, triangle or tetrahedron, formed by n+1 affinely independent points.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a light secondary stress on the second. The final 'x' is pronounced 'ks', and the vowel in 'plex' is short, as in 'pep'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term
nuance.usage_note: Americans use simplex mainly in mathematics, computer science and engineering. In data science and optimization, it refers to the simplex method, a classic algorithm for linear programming. In everyday talk the word is rare and would be understood only by specialists.

distinctions.note: A simplex is a single shape, while a simplicial complex is a collection of simplices glued together along faces.
Simplex is the shape in geometry; simplex method is the optimization algorithm that moves along the edges of such shapes.

examples.everyday: My cousin explained that a triangle is a two-dimensional simplex, which made sense to me after all.
examples.professional: We used the simplex method to solve the resource allocation problem in the model.
examples.analytical: A simplex is defined as the convex hull of affinely independent points, and this definition generalizes the triangle to any dimension.

nuance.analogy: A simplex is like the smallest possible building block for a shape: one point, a line, a triangle, a tetrahedron, and so on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin simplex, 'single' or 'simple'.
common_mistakes: Confusing simplex with simplicity
Pronouncing the final 'x' as 'sh' or 'z'
Using simplex as a synonym for simple

simplex.etymology: The adjective is a Latin *simplex* (“plain, simple; single”).

senses.definition: From a specified time in the past.
senses.example: I met him last year, but haven't seen him since.

senses.definition: From: referring to a period of time ending in the present and defining it by the point in time at which it started, or the period in which its starting point occurred.
senses.example: I'd known her only since the previous year, so from/since the moment we got married we’ve quarreled.

senses.definition: Continuously during that period of time.
senses.example: I'd known her only since the previous year, so from/since the moment we got married we’ve quarreled.

senses.definition: At certain points during that period of time.
senses.example: The team has changed its coach several times since 2015.

senses.definition: From the time that.
senses.example: I have loved you since I first met you.

senses.definition: Because.
senses.example: Since you didn't call, we left without you.

core.definition: From a specified time in the past until now, or from a particular point up to the present.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with a short i and a clear final s. Don't add a t sound as in 'sinst' or a schwa as in 'sin-uhs'; the n goes straight into the s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use since constantly to talk about a starting point in time, such as 'I've lived here since 2019.' With a full clause it means 'from the time that' or 'because', and in casual speech it often sounds like 'cause'. A common natural reply to 'Since when?' is a short answer like 'Since last week.'

distinctions.note: Since is used with a starting point (since Monday), while for is used with a length of time (for three days).
Because gives a cause and is used with clauses; since, in its causal sense, is more formal and written and usually sounds softer.

examples.everyday: I've been craving tacos since lunch, so let's go out tonight.
examples.professional: The client has been waiting for a revised quote since Monday, so please send it today.
examples.analytical: Since the argument depends on an assumed premise, its conclusion is only as strong as that premise.

nuance.analogy: Like a timer that started at a set moment and is still running now.
nuance.etymology: Shortened from Middle English sithen, from Old English siththan, 'after that'.
common_mistakes: Using since with a duration: say 'for two years' (I've lived here for two years), not 'since two years'.
Using since with a simple past tense when the action continues: say 'I've lived here since 2019', not 'I lived here since 2019'.

since.etymology: From Middle English *syns*, *synnes*, contraction of earlier *sithens*, *sithence*, from *sithen* (“after, since”) ( + *-s*, adverbial genitive suffix), from Old English *sīþþan*, from the phrase, from *sīþ* (“since, after”) + *þǣm* dative singular of *þæt*.

senses.definition: Having sinned; guilty of sin.
Constituting a sin; morally or religiously wrong; wicked; evil.
senses.example: Lying to the grieving family about the accident was a sinful act that he could not justify.

senses.definition: Decadent (luxuriously self-indulgent)
senses.example: The hotel's sinful spa menu offered chocolate baths and champagne breakfasts every morning.

core.definition: Morally wrong, or having done something wrong; also, pleasurably indulgent in a way that feels like a guilty pleasure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a syllabic 'l' with almost no vowel, so it sounds like 'SIN-fuhl' with the l carrying the sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative in religious or moral contexts; playful in casual talk about indulgent food or treats.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, sinful is often used playfully for rich food or desserts, as in 'this cake is sinful.' In religious or moral discussion it is serious and strong. Using it about a person's character in a secular setting may sound judgmental or preachy.

distinctions.note: Wicked is stronger and more dramatic, often suggesting evil intent, while sinful usually refers to moral failure measured against a standard.
Immoral is a general secular term for conduct that violates ethical principles, while sinful usually has a religious frame.

examples.everyday: Eating a whole pie for breakfast felt sinful, but it was worth it.
examples.professional: Hiding the audit logs to protect the launch date was sinful, even if nobody said it out loud.
examples.analytical: Augustine argued that a sinful will cannot save itself apart from grace.

nuance.analogy: Calling something sinful is like a red line on a map: it marks a boundary you know you should not cross.
nuance.etymology: From Old English synfull, from sin with the suffix -ful, meaning full of sin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'ful' like 'fool' instead of a light 'fuhl'.
Using sinful for any mistake, when it is more serious and moral in meaning.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek New Testament, the word hamartōlos (sinner, sinful) describes people who are in a state of sin. In Luke 5:8 Peter says he is a sinful man in the presence of Jesus, showing a sense of unworthiness before God. Romans 3:23 says all have sinned, and Romans 5:8 says Christ died for us while we were still sinners, which together frame sinfulness as universal and answered by grace.

traditions.view: Sin is understood mainly as missing the mark of human communion with God and a disease of the soul, with ancestral sin seen as inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt.
Sin is an offense against God that requires repentance and forgiveness, and original sin is inherited as a wound of nature that is removed by baptism, though concupiscence remains.

Sin is a condition of rebellion against God that corrupts the whole person, and Lutherans and Reformed Christians differ on whether inherited sin is primarily guilt or also a corrupt nature, with Reformed views often stressing total depravity.

sinful.etymology: From Middle English *synful*, *senful*, *sunful*, from Old English *synful* (“sinful, guilty, wicked, corrupt”), equivalent to *sin* + *ful*.

senses.definition: The cardinal number immediately following sixty-three and preceding sixty-five.

core.definition: The cardinal number 64, which comes after sixty-three and before sixty-five.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOUR, and the r is pronounced clearly in American speech. The 'ty' in 'sixty' is reduced to a light 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain number.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sixty-four for counting, measurements, and technical contexts such as computing, where 64-bit systems are common. The number is said in the same way in both everyday and technical speech.

distinctions.note: Sixty-six is two higher, so it is a different number even though the spellings look similar.
Sixty-fourth is the ordinal form, used for position, such as the sixty-fourth floor.

examples.everyday: That old laptop has sixty-four gigabytes, so it's plenty for photos.
examples.professional: We're migrating the service to sixty-four bit architecture to handle larger datasets.
examples.analytical: The chessboard has sixty-four squares, which makes it a natural example for discussing combinatorial growth.

nuance.analogy: Sixty-four is like a chessboard: a neat, complete grid of squares.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final r weakly or dropping it, which changes the word in American speech.
Confusing sixty-four with sixty-six when reading numbers aloud.

senses.definition: To cause (a distribution) to be asymmetrical.
senses.example: Outliers in the sample can skew the distribution toward the right, so we should check them first.

senses.definition: To form or shape in an oblique way; to cause to take an oblique position.
senses.example: The wind had skewed the old barn roof so that its ridge tilted sharply to one side.

senses.definition: To bias or distort in a particular direction.
senses.example: A disproportionate number of female subjects in the study group skewed the results.

senses.definition: To move obliquely; to move sideways, to sidle; to lie obliquely.
senses.example: The stray cat skewed sideways along the fence, keeping an eye on the dog.

senses.definition: To jump back or sideways in fear or surprise; to shy, as a horse.
senses.example: The mare skewed sideways at the sudden blast of the train whistle and nearly threw her rider.

senses.definition: To look at obliquely; to squint; hence, to look slightingly or suspiciously.
senses.example: He skewed his eyes at the salesman, plainly doubting every word of the pitch.

senses.definition: Of a distribution: asymmetrical about its mean.
senses.example: The income data is heavily skewed, with a few very high earners pulling the average up.

senses.definition: Neither parallel nor perpendicular to a certain line; askew.
senses.example: a skew arch

senses.definition: Of two lines in three-dimensional space: neither intersecting nor parallel.
senses.example: In our geometry homework, we proved that the two lines were skew, not parallel.

senses.definition: A state of asymmetry in a distribution; skewness.
senses.example: The analysis reported a skew of 1.4, confirming a long tail on the right.

senses.definition: Something that has an oblique or slanted position.
senses.example: The picture on the wall had a slight skew, so I straightened it.

senses.definition: An oblique or sideways movement.
senses.example: With a quick skew of his shoulders, he slipped past the crowded doorway.

senses.definition: A squint or sidelong glance.
senses.example: She gave the suspicious man a sharp skew before turning back to her coffee.

senses.definition: A kind of wooden vane or cowl in a chimney which revolves according to the direction of the wind and prevents smoking.
senses.example: The old farmhouse chimney had a wooden skew that spun whenever the wind changed.

senses.definition: A piece of rock lying in a slanting position and tapering upwards which overhangs a working-place in a mine and is liable to fall.
senses.example: The miners checked the skew overhanging the drift before anyone walked beneath it.

senses.definition: A bias or distortion in a particular direction.
senses.example: Critics said the survey's question wording introduced a political skew into the results.

senses.definition: A phenomenon in synchronous digital circuit systems (such as computers) in which the same sourced clock signal arrives at different components at different times.
senses.example: Clock skew between the two chips caused intermittent errors in our synchronous design.

senses.definition: A thick drizzling rain or driving mist.
senses.example: A cold skew of driving mist swept over the moors all afternoon.

senses.definition: A stone at the foot of the slope of a gable, the offset of a buttress, etc. cut with a sloping surface and with a check to receive the coping stones and retain them in place; a skew-corbel.
(rare) Askew, obliquely; awry.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To make something lopsided or tilted, or to distort a set of data or results so that it leans in one direction.

pronunciation.tip: Use a single long oo sound that starts with a y glide, as in 'skyoo'. Do not add an extra vowel between the k and the y.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use, but negative when it describes data or results that are distorted by bias.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people use skew to mean a tilt or angle, such as 'the picture is skewed.' In data work, Americans say that a result is skewed by outliers or bias. Using skew for a deliberate distortion of facts can sound critical.

distinctions.note: Skew describes a lopsided shape or distribution, while bias usually describes a systematic error or unfair influence on results.

examples.everyday: The photo came out a little skewed, so I straightened it.
examples.professional: The outliers in last quarter's sales data skewed our average upward, so we switched to the median.
examples.analytical: A sample drawn only from volunteers can skew the conclusions in ways that the statistics alone may not reveal.

nuance.analogy: Skewing is like leaning a picture frame on the wall, so that one side sits lower than the other.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'skewen' (to turn aside), of uncertain origin, possibly from Old French 'eschiuer'.
common_mistakes: Using 'skew' as a noun in everyday speech; the common noun is 'skew' in technical use only.
Pronouncing it as 'skoo', which drops the y sound.

skew.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *skeuen*, *skewe*, *skewen* (“to run at an angle or obliquely; to escape”), from *escuer*, variants of Old French *eschuer*, *eschever*, *eschiver* (“to escape, flee; to avoid”), from **skiuhan* (“to dread; to avoid,…

senses.definition: A detective.
(rare) A group of bears.
senses.example: Rangers spotted a sleuth of bears feeding on berries near the creek.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To act as a detective; to try to discover who committed a crime, or, more generally, to solve a mystery.
senses.example: Determined to clear her name, Maria decided to sleuth through the company's old emails.

core.definition: A detective, especially an amateur or private investigator who solves mysteries or uncovers hidden facts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable. End with a voiceless 'th' as in 'truth', not a 't' or 'd', and keep the 'sl' cluster smooth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is often playful, admiring the skill of someone who digs out the truth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sleuth for amateur detectives, mystery novels, or people who investigate something online ('internet sleuths'). It is informal and a little playful, so it fits casual talk and news. As a verb, to sleuth out means to investigate or find out, as in 'We sleuthed out the source of the error.' In a police report, say detective or investigator.

distinctions.note: Detective is the general, neutral word for a police or private investigator; sleuth is more informal and suggests cleverness in solving a puzzle.
Investigator is formal and used in professional or official contexts; sleuth is informal and more colorful.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a total sleuth, and she figured out who keeps taking our packages from the porch.
examples.professional: We need someone with a sleuth's patience to trace where the duplicate records came from.
examples.analytical: The historian becomes a sleuth, reconstructing a hidden motive from scattered letters and account books.

nuance.analogy: A sleuth is like a bloodhound following a scent: patient, methodical, and focused on one trail until it leads somewhere.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse slóð, meaning track or trail; the detective sense comes from sleuth-hound, a bloodhound used for tracking.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a /t/ or /d/ sound instead of the voiceless 'th'.
Using sleuth as a formal word in official reports, where detective or investigator is more natural.

senses.definition: One who slumbers; a sleeper.

core.definition: A person who is sleeping or who sleeps, often used in a gentle or poetic way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SLUM. The middle and last syllables are both reduced, with the final 'er' pronounced as a light American r-colored schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It sounds gentle and peaceful, and is usually used in poetry or descriptive writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'slumberer' in everyday speech; they say 'sleeper,' 'someone who's asleep,' or 'a deep sleeper.' You will mostly find it in literature, poetry, or old-fashioned descriptions. If you need a common word in conversation, use 'sleeper' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Sleeper' is the everyday word for a person who sleeps; 'slumberer' is literary and suggests a quiet, peaceful sleep.
An insomniac has trouble sleeping, while a slumberer is someone who is peacefully asleep.

examples.professional: Our on-call engineer is a light slumberer, so we set the pager to vibrate instead of ringing.
examples.analytical: The poem treats the sleeping village as a community of slumberers, quiet and yet watched over.

nuance.analogy: A slumberer is a sleeper seen through a softer lens, like a cat dozing in the afternoon sun.
nuance.etymology: From slumber (verb) plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Using 'slumberer' in casual speech, where 'sleeper' sounds more natural.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'slum-BER-er.'

senses.definition: One who practices sodomy; a sodomist.
A native or inhabitant of Sodom.

core.definition: A person who engages in sodomy; in Scripture, a native or inhabitant of the city of Sodom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa, so it sounds like SAH-duh-mite, not SO-doh-mite. Because it is an offensive slur for gay men, avoid using it casually.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and offensive; as a slur against gay men it is hurtful, and in biblical contexts it refers to people of Sodom.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English this word is treated as a slur, so avoid it in conversation and writing about sexuality. Scholars and translators use it mainly when discussing history or the older use of the term. In Bible study, say 'people of Sodom' or 'men of Sodom' instead.

distinctions.note: Sodom is the ancient city named in Genesis; sodomite is a term for its people or, in later usage, a pejorative label.
Sodomy is the act or the legal term; sodomite is the person, and is now considered a slur.

examples.everyday: That word is a slur, so please don't call people sodomites.
examples.professional: The commentary notes that 'sodomite' became a slur, so modern translations avoid it when rendering Genesis 19.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers used 'sodomite' to label a whole category of sinners, a usage that reads Genesis 19 far more narrowly than the text itself does.

nuance.analogy: Like a word that once described a place of origin but later became a weapon, its meaning now carries the harm of the label.
nuance.etymology: From Sodom, the Biblical city, plus the suffix -ite meaning a native or follower of.
common_mistakes: Using the word as a neutral description of a person's identity, which is offensive.
Stressing the second syllable, saying SO-doh-mite.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is Sᵊdōm (סְדֹם), the city destroyed with Gomorrah. Genesis 19:1-29 describes men of the city surrounding Lot's house and the city's destruction by fire. Ezekiel 16:49 lists Sodom's sins as pride, abundance of food, and neglect of the poor and needy, not sexual acts alone. Jude 1:7 refers to Sodom and Gomorrah as a warning about going after strange flesh.

sodomite.etymology: From Middle English *sodomyte*, *sodomite*, from Old French *Sodomite* and Latin *sodomīta*, from Ancient Greek *σοδομίτης*.

senses.definition: A formal evening party.

core.definition: A formal evening party, often with music, conversation or art, held in a private home or elegant venue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, RAY. The first syllable is SWAH, not SWEE or SOY. Americans usually drop the French accent and pronounce the final syllable as a clear long A.

nuance.connotation: Positive but slightly fancy. It suggests an elegant gathering and can sound pretentious for a casual party.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soiree for an upscale evening gathering, often in a home or at a cultural venue, sometimes with music, wine or art. It is more common in writing, invitations and news about social events than in casual talk. For ordinary parties, say 'party', 'get-together' or 'gathering'; a natural reply to an invitation is 'Thanks for inviting me, I'd love to come.'

distinctions.note: Party is the general, everyday word for any social gathering. Soiree is more formal and suggests elegance or culture.
A gala is a large, festive event, often a fundraiser with a dress code. A soiree is usually smaller and more intimate.
A reception is a formal event after a ceremony, such as a wedding or award. A soiree is an evening gathering held for its own sake.

examples.everyday: Are you going to Maria's soiree on Saturday, or is it too fancy for you?
examples.professional: The firm is hosting a soiree for clients at the art museum on Thursday evening.
examples.analytical: The nineteenth-century salon soiree shaped literary reputations as much as the printed review did.

nuance.analogy: A soiree is like a candlelit dinner party with music and conversation, where guests dress up and mingle.
nuance.etymology: From French soirée, meaning evening or evening party, from soir, meaning evening.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it SWEE-ray or SOY-ree, instead of swah-RAY.
Using soiree for a casual backyard gathering, which sounds odd and overly formal.

senses.definition: Completely sold; of which no more is in stock.
senses.example: The concert tickets were sold out within ten minutes of going on sale.

core.definition: Having no more left for sale, because all of the stock or tickets have been bought.

pronunciation.tip: Put primary stress on OUT, as in sohld OWT, and keep the d lightly before OUT. Don't add a vowel between the two words; the d links into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for tickets or popular products, and mildly negative when a customer just missed out.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sold out for concerts, games, restaurants, and popular products, often in the form 'Sorry, we're sold out.' As an adjective before a noun, write sold-out. A natural reply might be 'Do you know when more will be available?' or 'Could you put me on the waitlist?'

distinctions.note: Out of stock means the item is temporarily unavailable and may be restocked; sold out often implies high demand for an item or event that is gone for now.
Discontinued means the product is no longer made; sold out only means the current supply is finished.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the concert is sold out, but the resale site might still have a few seats.
examples.professional: Marketing says the spring webinar is sold out, so let's schedule a second session before the end of the month.
examples.analytical: To call a product sold out is to describe a temporary state of exhausted supply, not a permanent decision about its future.

nuance.analogy: Like a bakery shelf that is empty by noon: the bread is still baked, but the day's supply has gone out the door.
nuance.etymology: Compound of sold, the past tense of sell, and out.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sold out' without 'of' before a noun; use 'sold out of milk' or 'sold out of tickets.'
Writing 'sold-out' before a noun only when it is an adjective; the hyphen is for the attributive use.

conversation.text: Sorry, the small sizes are sold out, but we're getting more Friday.
The concert sold out in ten minutes, so we didn't get tickets.
Sorry, we're sold out of the pumpkin bread today. Come back tomorrow?

senses.definition: Eventually, at some undetermined time in the not-too-distant future.
senses.example: He’ll turn up sooner or later.

core.definition: Eventually; at some point in the future, though you do not know exactly when.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SOON and LAY, and reduce 'or' to a quick 'er'. The t in 'later' is a flap, so it sounds like 'LAY-der' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sooner or later in casual talk, at work and in writing, often to predict something unpleasant or inevitable. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know' or 'You're right, we'll see.' It is informal but polite in most situations.

distinctions.note: Eventually is more neutral and formal; sooner or later adds a sense of inevitability and is more conversational.
Someday usually refers to a wish or a distant hope, while sooner or later suggests something that will certainly happen.

collocations: it will come out sooner or later
we'll find out sooner or later

examples.everyday: At the restaurant, my son asked for dessert, and I told him he'd get it sooner or later.
examples.professional: Sooner or later the vendor will have to explain why the deployment slipped again.
examples.analytical: Sooner or later every false premise in an argument will be exposed by its consequences.
